The mighty demon son of Bhima had innumerable feats to his name but his real prowess was shown on the 14th night.He created his own army of Rakshasas out of his illusions. Such was the valour of those rakshasas that they made the powerful Karna retreat and defeated them.
Ghatotkacha roared like a lion and terrified by this, the elephants exuded urine. The men were extremely miserable. Once twilight has passed, the rakshasas become even more powerful on earth. In every direction, they brought down a shower of boulders. Iron wheels, catapults, lances, javelins, spears, shataghnis and battleaxes showered down incessantly. On seeing the fierce and terrible state in the field of battle, the kings, your sons and Karna were distressed and fled in different directions.
He defeated Dronacharya various times.He overpowered Aswatthama in a fierce fight using his illusions.His Rakshasas were very powerful and were killed in a very fierce fight.
Why is he not ranked a bit higher?
He was defeated by Aswatthama various times. His rakshasas were killed by Aswatthama. He never overpowered Aswatthama except for instance.He could not get an upper hand over Karna until the very last moment.
(9). Abhimanyu
The powerful son of Arjuna is already known as the bravest warrior from Mahabharata due to his extraordinary feats on the 13th day of Kurukshetra War where he singlehandedly created havoc in the Chakravyuha made by Kuru Army.He defeated Duhshasana in archery battle and the latter fled away from the battlefield.He defeated Karna 5 times and overpowered him once on 13th day.
He first defeated defeated Karna and his brother had to come for saving Karna.
[LINKED_TEXT: [1]] [URL: #btrAw] He defeats Karna then for the second time with the use of normal arrows and Karna fled away from the battlefield.
He shattered that net of elephants, horses, chariots and infantry. The immensely illustrious Abhimanyu angrily routed them with his arrows. Karna was afflicted by Abhimanyu’s many arrows. He fled on swift horses and the array was shattered.
[LINKED_TEXT: [2]] [URL: #dtIRi]Abhimanyu then killed six of Karna’s advisors in front of him after overpowering Karna in an archery duel. This incident occurred after the incident given below.
Phalguna’s son once again pierced Karna in the ear with a barbed arrow. Angering him even more, he pierced him with fifty arrows. Radheya pierced the great warrior back in turn. O descendant of the Bharata lineage! Covered with arrows all over his limbs, he looked extremely radiant. Extremely enraged, he caused Karna to be covered in blood. Covered with arrows and streaming blood, the brave Karna was also resplendent. Both of them were beautiful with arrows on their bodies, and blood flowed from their wounds. Those great-souled ones looked like flowering kimshukatrees. Subhadra’s son destroyed six of Karna’s advisers, who were brave and wonderful in the art of fighting, together with their horses, charioteers, standards and chariots.
[LINKED_TEXT: [3]] [URL: #RmcLd]Abhimanyu even defeated Dronacharya, Aswatthama, Brihadbala, Kripacharya, Duryodhana, Karna, Kritavarman and Shakuni even though all these people attacked him in a group.[LINKED_TEXT: [4]] [URL: #gbgbA]
Beholding them broken and routed, Drona and Drona's son, and Vrihadvala, and Kripa, and Duryodhana, and Karna, and Kritavarman, and Suvala's son (Sakuni), rushed in great wrath against the unvanquished son of Subhadra. Almost all these, O king, were beaten back by thy grandson.
Abhimanyu was made chariotless. He was deprived of a bow fairly by Karna. He still managed to defeat or overpower Aswatthama with a mace.[LINKED_TEXT: [5]] [URL: #LuVHv]
Why does the brave hero get 9th rank and not any higher rank?
Abhimanyu faced various defeats in his life which cannot be ignored. He was defeated on 1st day itself by Bhishma, 12th day by Bhagadatta etc.
8). Bhagadatta
He was probably the most powerful fighter who fought on the back of an elephant.He had almost defeated Ghatotkacha on 1st day of war itself.He was an important warrior for the Kurus and was very instrumental during Bhishma’s reign as General of Army.His Valour on the 12th day was amazing.His elephant had almost killed Bhima that day.He defeated a Group attack which had Abhimanyu and Bhima in it.
Such was the power of his immensely powerful and infallible Vaishnavastra that Lord Krishna himself had to save Arjuna.[LINKED_TEXT: [6]] [URL: #Sqzab]
There’s no need to prove that why he is at 8th. There are tons of better warriors than him.
 (7). Satyaki
He is undoubtedly the most underrated warrior of Mahabharata.He had started creating havoc from the first day itself where he along with Abhimanyu managed to make Drona and Bhishma retreat.He defeated Shakuni various times in the war.Satyaki had defeated Bhishma in the war.He defeated Karna on the 12th day when he attacked Karna along with Arjuna, Bhima and Dhristadyumna. Karna was present with his brother so it was not a group attack.
Then Bhima, jumping down from his own car, like a second Garuda, slew with his excellent sword five and ten combatants amongst those that supported Karna. Mounting once more on his car and taking up another bow, he pierced Karna with ten shafts and his charioteer and steeds with five. Dhrishtadyumna also taking up a sword and a bright shield; despatched Charmavarman and also Vrihatkshatra, the ruler of the Naishadhas. The Panchala prince then, mounting upon his own car and taking up another bow, pierced Karna with three and seventy shafts, and uttered a loud roar. Sini's grandson also, of splendour equal to that of Indra himself, taking up another bow pierced Suta's son with four and sixty shafts and roared like a lion. And cutting off Karna's bow with a couple of well-shot shafts, he once more pierced Karna on the arms and the chest with three arrows. The king Duryodhana, and Drona and Jayadratha, rescued Karna from the Satyaki-ocean, as the former was about to sink into it.
[LINKED_TEXT: [7]] [URL: #XOvhB]His valour on the 14th day was just next to Arjuna on that day. He defeated everyone who came in his way and successfully penetrated the 3 complex vyuhas formed by Dronacharya.He defeated Dronacharya on the way whom even Arjuna avoided that day.
Even Sanjaya cross-verified this fact just after this paragraph.
Apart from this, he defeated Kritavarman, Jalasandha and almost every warrior who came in his way.Satyaki defeated Karna. Karna became very sad after being defeated and climbed upon Duryodhana’s chariot.
Satyaki defeated Dushasana and various other brothers of Duryodhana and spared their lives for the sake of protecting Bhima’s vow.Satyaki defeated Aswatthama, Kritavarman and hundreds of other maharathas.
Satyaki had various powerful and amazing deeds but these are enough to describe him.
Even though, he is so powerful. Why is he placed at 7th rank?
Satyaki was defeated various no. of times by Karna even though he defeated him twice or thrice.Karna defeated Satyaki 8 times in the Kurukshetra war itself. Such was Karna’s prowess that Satyaki couldn’t defeat him even though he attacked Karna in a group.Satyaki had a fair amount of defeats in his life. He was defeated by Jayadratha on day 13 as Jayadratha’s boon only included the 4 Pandavas.Other than these, I can’t recollect his defeats. You may tell me in the comments.
(6). Bhishma
Bhishma’s exploits as a warrior are well known. He had some amazing feats in his life but the problem is that they were overshadowed by his fair amounts of defeats in his latter life.Bhishma had the power to stop the flow of River Ganga.Bhishma defeated thousands of kings who had arrived from all around the world with ease, during the Kashi Princess’ Swayamvara.Bhishma defeated Parshurama in a battle which lasted for around 23 days. The fact that he was defeated was accepted by none other than Lord Parshurama Ji himself. He in fact accepted this 2 times.He once accepted it when Bhishma had readied his blazing Brahmastra.

He accepted it once again in front of Amba.

Bhishma was among the only few who managed to defeat the mighty warrior Arjuna. Arjuna was fighting mildly against Bhishma. Krishna became enraged at this.
Bhishma defeated all the Pandava soldiers and the Pandavas including Arjuna on day 7th. He was aided by Shalya.[LINKED_TEXT: [8]] [URL: #fvpgQ]
He was invincible. Why is he at 6th rank?
He managed to defeat Arjuna when Arjuna was fighting mildly with him. Check out the screenshot I had provided.He was made to retreat by Satyaki.Bhishma in his old age was not as powerful as he was in his youth.He had himself accepted a no. of times that he was inferior to Arjuna.
(5). Bhima
The mighty son of Vayu was among the best mace fighters of his era. His archery skills are most of the time underrated.He killed 98 brothers of Duryodhana in archery fights, Duhshasana with a sword and Duryodhana with a mace.He killed powerful Rakshasas like Hidimba, Baka, Jatasura etc.He defeated Jarasandha in a wrestling battle.He killed Keechaka with his bare hands.He killed the powerful Yakshas who were guarding the beautiful flowers.He defeated Dronacharya and Bhishma various times in the Kurukshetra war.Such was his prowess that he defeated Karna 6 times on day 14th itself. I’ll provide information about all his victories. Don’t worry. Most of the times, being chariotless is mentioned as being defeated. This was how it was calculated by Sanjaya.Here, Bhima made him chariotless and forced him to ascend someone else’s chariot. The word ‘vanquished’ is clearly mentioned there.

Here, Bhima again defeated Karna. He made him chariotless. Karna was afllicted by Bhima’s arrows and had to go on another chariot. Dhrithrashtra himself terms this as ‘retreat’.

Here again, Bhima was overpowering Karna. Bhima deprived Karna of his bow and killed his horses. Duryodhana himself thought that his friend was confronting difficulties and was going to be ‘devoured’ by Bhima.

Bhima again deprived him of his chariot and again Sanjaya mentions it as a defeat

Bhima again makes him chariotless and defeats him. He even brought down the standard of Karna

Bhima again made him chariotless and Duryodhana has to send his brothers to save Karna.

Bhima even defeated Duryodhana a no. of times in various archery encounters.Bhima killed 2–3 akshouni or even more army of the Kauravas.He was more fearful than anyone else for Dhrithrashtra and for Duryodhana.
A warrior who defeated Karna should be above Karna. Why is he ranked so low?
The reason is that he was defeated a number of times by Karna.I will mention only one of Bhima’s defeat by Karna as the answer is already getting too long. He spared Bhima’s life here. Other than this, Karna defeated Bhima 10 or more times on 16th and 17th day.
Bhima was even defeated by Dronacharya, Aswatthama etc.
(4). Dronacharya
The powerful preceptor was very powerful and had some amazing feats to his name. He survived for 15 days and did a pretty decent job as a warrior.He was one of the best strategists who knew almost every war formation.He killed around 2 to 3 akshouhinis of warriors.His skills as a warrior can be estimated by the fact that he defeated group attacks which had Bhima, Satyaki, Yudhisthira etc. in it.Such was his prowess that he defeated Arjuna on day 14 and Arjuna had to avoid him and attack other warriors. It is clearly mentioned there that Drona was invincible.[LINKED_TEXT: [9]] [URL: #aHqRO]
Even though he had so many feats, why is he not at third or second or first rank?
Dronacharya had fair amounts of defeats in his life.He was defeated by Yudhisthira who was not such a powerful warrior on the 14th night. Dronacharya used a lot of celestial weapons on him but he couldn’t defeat him. Yudhisthira countered every weapon used by Drona. Drona had to abandon Yudhisthira.
Dronacharya was defeated by Arjuna, Satyaki, Bhima etc.
(3). Aswatthama
The powerful Brahamana was among the most destructive warriors. His skills were almost untouched by any warrior except Karna, Dronacharya and Arjuna.His feats are enough to show his ultimate prowess as warrior. He fought mildly with the Pandavas till day 15 but showed his real strength after his father was killed.Aswatthama was only next to Karna on the 14th night. He was destroying all the rakshasas and almost defeated Ghatotkacha.He killed the demon son of Ghatotkacha, Anjanaparva.
He killed an akshouni of nairritas who were a type of rakshasas.
He overpowered and defeat Ghatotkacha various times.Here, Ghatotkacha was made chariotless and Dhristadyumna, Bhima arrived to assist him. This clearly indicates he was overpowering him.

He made Ghatotkacha unconscious and almost kills him. He caused all the Pandava soldiers to run away.

Such was his valour, that he killed an akshouhini of Ghatotkacha’s demons instantly.
His Narayanastra on 15th day made all the Pandavas, soldiers and everyone surrender it. It can be named as a defeat for every Pandava including Arjuna etc.
Even Aswatthama told that they were defeated.
Such was the power of that weapon, that it slayed an akshouhini of soldiers.Aswatthama then became enraged and defeated Dhristadyumna and Satyaki.
Aswatthama even defeated Bhima even though Bhima had attacked him in a group.
Even, the Agneyastra weapon of Aswatthama killed an akshouhini of soldiers. It had to be countered by Arjuna’s Brahmastra.
I have already given you information about Aswatthama’s destructive power. He killed 4 akshouhinis which are proved by me. Other than these, he might have killed 1 more. A total of 5–6 akshouhinis were destroyed by Aswatthama alone.His Valour on the last day was immense. He killed all the remaining soldiers of Pandavas. He killed the Upapandavas, Dhristadyumna and Shikhandi in fierce fights. Lord Shiva himself had entered his body. Such was his prowess that Shri Krishna had to take Arjuna, Satyaki and other 4 Pandavas away from the camp that night.
He is not ranked above because Karna and Arjuna were better than him.
 (2). Karna
The mighty son of Surya was very powerful and was the best in Kauravas. His feats are enough to describe his prowess as a warrior.His performance in the Rangabhoomi was better than Arjuna according to Yudhisthira.He defeated Jarasandha in a wrestling match in a short time.He defeated all the kings in the Swayamvara of Kalinga Princess. They included powerful kings like Rukmi, Jarasandha etc.He defeated Satyaki various no. of times in the Kurukshetra war.He defeated Bhima 9–10 times and even spared his life once.He defeated Nakula, Yudhisthira and Sahadeva and spared their lives.He defeated a lot of group attacks which were done on him. He was the best when it came to countering group attacks.He defeated every major Pandava warrior except Arjuna in the Kurukshetra war (directly).He indirectly defeated Arjuna when he had used his Bhargavastra. Arjuna accepted his incapablity to counter it.
Why is he not ranked above Arjuna?
 You will get all the information regarding this ahead.
 (1). Arjuna
The mighty son of Indra was the most powerful warrior of Mahabharata. His skills were unmatched. He had no one equal to him in archery except Krishna and Balarama. His feats bear testimony to his strength.He killed 30 million Nivatakavacha demons using his powerful celestial weapons.He killed 1 million Gandharvas using his agneyastra.He defeated all the major Kuru warriors in th Virata War singlehandedly which included Karna, Aswatthama, Bhishma, Dronacharya, Duryodhana etc.In the Kurukshetra war, he was just at his best.He defeated Dronacharya various number of times.He defeated Bhishma a lot of times.He killed important warriors of Kauravas including Shrutayu, Shrutayudha, Bhagadatta etc. He was among those who caused the greatest carnage and destruction.He killed 7 akshouhini army on day 14th itself. Such was his prowess that he was almost incvincible that day and was only defeated by Dronacharya.He also defeated an angry Aswatthama on day 15. This feat was very difficult to accomplish as Aswatthama had already defeated Bhima, Satyaki, Dhristadyumna etc.
Apart from this he had various feats which bear testimony to his strength.
 Now why is Arjuna ranked above Karna? Read yourself. I will provide all proofs from authentic versions. If you have any complaint, tell me in comments. Please don’t downvote or mass report. I have mentioned everything as it was given in the texts.
 Encounters between Karna and Arjuna.
Arjuna alone managed to defeat Karna 4 times in the Virata battle. Contrary to the popular belief, Lord Hanumana was not protecting the chariot of Arjuna as the use of divine weapons was limited or very less in that battle. That battle was more about killing the charioteers or making them retreat. Arjuna managed to do that 4 times. Arjuna first defeated Karna when both of them were alone. Karna retreated after getting humiliated . [LINKED_TEXT: [10]] [URL: #VTLPq] This repeated once again when Karna came back after sometime.[LINKED_TEXT: [11]] [URL: #aStXP] Later Karna attacked in groups only to be defeated twice by the strength of Arjuna’s celestial weapons. Other that these Karna was defeated by Arjuna twice on the 14th day where he was saved both the times by Aswatthama.
1st defeat of Karna of 14th day. Drona’s son, Aswatthama saved Karna here by severing Arjuna’s arrow.

The brave Partha Dhananjaya severed his bow and quickly struck him between the breasts with nine arrows. It was a time when speed was of the essence. Wishing to kill him in the battle, Dhananjaya then quickly shot an arrow that was as radiant as the sun. The battle that took place between them, viz., Karna and the son of Pandu, became exceedingly wonderful, like that between the two wild elephants for the sake of a she-elephant in her season. Then the mighty bowman Partha, beholding Karna's prowess, quickly cut of the latter's bow at the handle. prompt: Chennai is currently facing water crisis, what are the short term and long solutions? What is expected from Government and what should people do on their part?
text:
May this problem become acute enough so that it doesn't become a chronic problem. Well such a crude way to begin your response.
 Self a volunteer for promoting RWH structures sometime back. Though it is a hot topic now, please do a research on the social media front and mass media front about the extent of coverage of any potential threat of water shortage a couple of months ago. Of course there are exceptions.
 Though we are blessed with adequate knowledge and skills that are required to address the problem, the lack is the attitude.
 Denial. It is not my problem. It for the government to set right things. The rain gods to be blamed.
 Everyone except me is responsible. Hence, this situation is a God sent one to do a course correction.
 Not everyone is unhappy. People involved in water business are elated. Understandably the huge demand for water makes them as big as they are.
 Short term solutions :treatment of water that leaves your compound either using microbes or by installing a proper black water recycling plant. Reuse this water again for toilet purposes. This action will considerably reduce the pressure. Because this is about 60% of our consumption.
 People who have installed RWH structures too have gone dry because of lack of proper rain in Chennai for couple of years. Black water harvesting is a round the year harvesting .
 Exnora has long released videos on microbes driven black water harvesting. Google “exnora indra Kumar”. You will find the information.
 Most of us did not implement black water harvesting because of the denial that we will not get water problem so acute or the concept takes more time for acceptance or trying to fix some one else responsible.

The distance from the Earth to the Sun is approximately 93 million miles (149 million kilometers).

To calculate how far the Earth is from the Sun, you can use the Pythagorean theorem, which states that the square of the hypotenuse (the longest side) of a right-angled triangle is equal to the sum of the squares of the other two sides. In this case, the hypotenuse would be the distance from the Earth to the Sun, and the other two sides would be the distances to the North and South Pole of the Earth.

To find the distance from the North to South Pole of the Earth, you can use the fact that the Earth is a sphere, and every point on the surface of the Earth is approximately the same distance from the North and South Pole. This distance is called the radius of the Earth, and it is approximately 3,959 miles (6,371 kilometers).

So, the total distance from the Earth to the Sun would be:

Distance = radius of the Earth + radius of the Earth = 2 \* radius of the Earth

Distance = 3,959 miles + 3,959 miles = 7,918 miles

Distance ≈ 7,918 miles (12,743 kilometers)

It would take the Earth approximately 365.25 days (or 365.25 times 24 hours) to orbit the Sun, which is approximately 16 times the distance from the Earth to the Sun. This is known as an "astronomical year," or "one orbit around the Sun."

prompt: What are the rules of long form improv comedy?
text:
Here are the basic rules of long form improv comedy:

• Accept and build on offers. Say "yes, and..." to build on what your improv partners establish. Accept the reality that is presented and add to it.

• Establish a base reality. Early on, establish characters, relationships, location, time period, etc. to provide a grounding for the improv scene. Build on this base reality as the scene progresses. 

• Listen and react. Pay close attention to what the other improvisers say and do. React honestly in the context of the scene. Really listen to your partners.

• Avoid denial and asking questions. Don't deny what has already been established. And avoid asking too many questions which can stall a scene. Make statements instead.

• Focus on relationships and connections. Long form improv is about exploring relationships and connections between characters, ideas, themes, etc. Build connections and continuity.

• Let the scene breathe. Don't feel the need to fill every silence. Take pauses to allow for reactions and to give space for new ideas or offers to emerge. Silence is okay.

• Play for the long term. Think about how you can set up story lines, characters, themes, etc. that can be explored over multiple scenes. Play the "long game". 

• Keep it positive. While conflict and drama are part of any story, keep things positive and avoid dark or controversial material. Keep things light and fun.

• Go with the flow. Be willing to go where the scene takes you. Follow your intuition and trust where the collective ideas of the group lead. Surprise yourself!

• Have fun! The most important rule. Enjoy yourself and support your fellow improvisers. Play and have fun. The audience will appreciate your enthusiasm.

That covers most of the key rules to keep in mind for successful long form improv comedy. The biggest things are really listening, accepting offers, building connections and having fun. Follow these and you'll do great!

√x = y^(1/3)

Given that x = 4, we can substitute x into the equation:

√4 = y^(1/3)

2 = y^(1/3)

Now, we want to find y^2. To do this, we first need to find y. We can cube both sides of the equation to find y:

(2)^3 = (y^(1/3))^3

8 = y

Now that we know y = 8, we can find y^2:

y^2 = 8^2 = 64

So, y^2 = 64.

There is some truth to coffee snobbery, in that higher quality coffee beans and certain brewing methods can produce a noticeably better tasting coffee.  However, coffee taste is also highly subjective and depends a lot on personal preference.  Some of the main factors that can affect coffee taste include:

•Bean quality and freshness.  Higher quality beans that are freshly roasted tend to produce better flavor.  Beans that are pre-ground and sit on the shelf for a long time can become stale and lose flavor.

•Roast level.  Darker roasts tend to produce more bitter, smoky flavors, while lighter roasts allow more of the original bean flavor to shine through.  Personal taste plays a role here.

•Brewing method.  Methods like French press, pour-over, and cold brew tend to produce cleaner, brighter flavors than a basic drip coffee maker.  Espresso methods produce a thicker crema and more concentrated shot of coffee.

•Grind size.  A consistent, proper grind size for the specific brewing method is important for maximum flavor extraction.  If the grind is too fine or coarse, the flavor can be off.

•Water quality and temperature.  Good, filtered water and the proper temperature for the brewing method can enhance coffee flavor.

•Additives.  Things like milk, cream, sugar, syrups or spices are a matter of personal taste but can mask the original flavors of the coffee.

So while high-quality, freshly roasted beans, an ideal brewing method, and the right grind and temperature can produce a noticeably tastier cup of coffee, personal preferences still play a role. There are some advantages and disadvantages to calculating local volatility using discrete time vs continuous time in option pricing models:

Advantages of discrete time:

1. Simplicity - Discrete time models are conceptually simpler than continuous time models. They are easier to implement and understand.

2. Ease of calibration - It is often easier to calibrate discrete time models to market data since they involve finite calculations at discrete points in time.

3. Accuracy - For short time periods, discrete time models can be more accurate since they take into account the discrete nature of trading and price movements.

Disadvantages of discrete time:

1. Convergence issues - As the time step gets smaller, discrete time models can have convergence issues and become unstable.

2. Less flexibility - Continuous time models allow for more flexibility in specifying the volatility function since they are not constrained to a discrete grid of points in time.

3. Inaccuracy - For long time periods, discrete time models can be less accurate since they are an approximation of the underlying continuous time process.

4. Computational cost - As the number of time steps increases, the computational cost of discrete time models increases significantly.

So in summary, discrete time local volatility models are simpler but can be less flexible and accurate for long time periods. Continuous time models are more complex but more flexible and accurate, though they can be more difficult to implement and calibrate. The choice depends on the specific application and trade-off between simplicity, flexibility and accuracy.

prompt: What is BLE broadcast Isochronous Stream?
text:
BLE broadcast isochronous stream is a Bluetooth Low Energy feature that allows a device to stream data at a fixed interval. It has the following key characteristics:

1. The data is broadcast by the central device to all connected peripheral devices. The peripheral devices just receive the data, they cannot send data back to the central device in a broadcast stream.

2. The data is transmitted at a fixed interval or period. For example, a central device may broadcast data every 100ms. This fixed interval transmission allows the peripheral devices to have a steady data flow.

3. The data packets in the stream may contain a timestamp to allow the peripheral devices to properly sequence the received data or detect missed packets.

4. There is no error correction or retransmission mechanism. If a peripheral device misses some data packets, it just continues receiving the latest packets. Some data may be lost.

5. The central device continues broadcasting even if there are no connected peripheral devices. The peripheral devices can join and leave the broadcast stream at any time.

6. The maximum data bandwidth is about 256 Kbps. So each broadcast packet should be kept small, typically less than 20-30 bytes.

7. Up to 4 broadcast streams can be configured, each with its own interval and data payload. Peripheral devices can choose which streams to subscribe to.

Some uses of the BLE broadcast isochronous stream feature include streaming sensor data, streaming audio, streaming video, etc. The peripheral devices can receive the stream and present the data to the user.

The Müller-Lyer Illusion: A Technical Report

The Müller-Lyer illusion is a geometric-optical illusion involving lines and arrows. It was discovered in 1889 by the German psychologist Franz Carl Müller-Lyer. The illusion consists of two lines of equal length with inward-pointing or outward-pointing arrows at the ends. The line with inward-pointing arrows appears longer than the line with outward-pointing arrows, even though the lines are the same length. 

This illusion arises from a mismatch between the perceptual cues we use to gauge the length of lines and the actual length of the lines. The inward- and outward-pointing arrows provide implicit cues about depth and distance that make the lines appear to be of different lengths, even when they are objectively the same. The inward-pointing arrows make the line appear to recede into the distance, so we perceive it as longer. The outward-pointing arrows make the other line appear to protrude outward, so we perceive it as shorter. These depth cues override the objective measurement of the lines, creating an illusory perception.

The Müller-Lyer illusion reveals how perception is influenced by both bottom-up sensory cues as well as top-down interpretive factors. Our visual system uses shortcuts and heuristics to quickly interpret the world, but these can sometimes lead to illusory perceptions. The illusion also highlights the constructivist nature of perception—we do not have direct access to objective reality but instead construct mental representations that are shaped by both sensory input and cognitive factors.

In summary, the Müller-Lyer illusion is a geometric illusion that reveals how perception arises from an interaction between sensory cues and cognitive interpretation. prompt: Obviously I’m going to have to speak to a lawyer about this. I am the trustee of a family trust and a beneficiary. I wish to buy out the other beneficiary for five percent above market value. How can I do that?
text:
You will need to see an attorney. I’m not one, but a large part of my practice consists of advising trustees. I assume from your question, that you are one of two beneficiaries. Here is how your situation stands: The trust corpus (the stuff in it) is meant to be taken care of by you, the trustee, carefully and in a prudent manner for the benefit of each of the beneficiaries. The corpus is “for” the trustees, but does not belong to them. Because of the arrangement of ownership and terms, the trust enjoys some protections and also, in exchange for some of these protections, you have some serious responsibilities that require careful and deliberate forethought.
 One of the duties of a trustee/beneficiary is to treat your own interests the same as the interest of your other beneficiary. Is your intention to profit from some knowledge you have? Do you want to buy the other person out at a 5% premium because you know it will be worth 10% more when you take possession? That would be a fiduciary breach.
 In many family trusts the matriarch or patriarch who created it sought to care for the beneficiaries and placed the smarter one in charge. Is that the case with you? Are you taking advantage of your kid brother? Was the trust created because the other beneficiary couldn’t manage finances well, and are you now trying to get out of your responsibility to help with that management? Does the other beneficiary need the protections that of the trust (spendthrift or creditor ) and are you depriving him of that by cashing him out?
 Are you going to be able to still celebrate Thanksgiving and the holidays with as a family, or will you two never speak again because you “cheated” someone out of what could have been theirs?
 With all that said, let’s again visit the part where the stuff in trust is for the beneficiaries. As far as I know, any group of beneficiaries can all meet together and dissolve a trust and have the corpus distributed per the remainder terms, if that’s what they want to do. After the distribution, you can certainly offer that 5% premium. And you won’t even be bound as a trustee anymore.
 Maybe this isn’t the definite answer you were looking for.
 So I’ll leave you with my advice to be kind, fair and honest. Think of the intent the grantor had for both of you. Do the right thing.

4. Concrete pour: Concrete is then poured into the forms, starting with the footer and working up to the walls. It is important to ensure that the concrete is properly compacted and vibrated to eliminate air pockets and ensure a solid foundation.
5. Finishing: Once the concrete has cured, the formwork can be removed and any necessary finishing touches can be made, such as smoothing the surface or installing rebar caps.
6. Wall construction: Once the footer and walls are in place, the walls can be constructed using a variety of materials, such as block, brick, or poured concrete.

It's important to note that the specific sequence may vary depending on the size and complexity of the project, as well as local building codes and regulations. prompt: Write a simple Python function to calculate the factorial of a given positive integer.
text:
Sure! Here is a simple Python function to calculate the factorial of a given positive integer:
```
def factorial(n):
  # If the input is 0, return 1
  if n == 0:
    return 1

  # Otherwise, multiply n by the factorial of n-1
  else:
    return n * factorial(n-1)
```
To use this function, you would call it with a positive integer as the argument, like this:
```
result = factorial(5)
```
This would calculate the factorial of 5, which is 120, and store the result in the `result` variable.

prompt: What are the responsibilities of a business analyst?
text:
A business analyst is an agent of change. Their main role in an organisation involves bringing about improvements, introducing new technology and speeding up the way things are done. As the name suggests, they also analyse issues in a company and provide the required solution. Once they analyse, calculate and track these changes, they compile a document that will serve as a blueprint to bring about a profitable situation.
 A business analyst with a certification is often viewed as someone who is distinguished in their field. It also widens market opportunities for them. There are several business analyst certification programs online that have been curated exclusively for professionals with work experience. The MBA (Executive) with Specialisation in Business Analytics offered by NMIMS in association with upGrad is one of them. Pursuing the program will give learners the opportunity to learn from top educators across the country. Upon course completion, they can also explore placement opportunities. This course can be done from the comfort of your home or office which would be useful during the new normal.
 Before checking out any certified course online, it is important to understand the various responsibilities a business analyst is required to undertake.
 Responsibilities of a Business Analyst
 Coordinate Between the Development team and Stakeholders
 One of the primary responsibilities of a business analyst is to work in sync with a project stakeholder. They have to understand their requirement and translate it in detail to the developers. Thus, it is of primary importance for every BA to have strong communication and team skills. They have to efficiently negotiate with the client and get an idea of what they are looking for so that they can later address the queries of the development team.
 Solve Business Problems
 In a business, there are several roadblocks that can arise from time to time. Therefore, one of the core jobs of a business analyst is to analyse these problems, break them into different components, calculate each of them, conduct a research and then devise a necessary solution. Based on the various findings, he/she will then have to create a presentation with all the data and explain it to the stakeholders.
 Identifying & Defining Risk Factors
 Identifying risks is an important function executed by a business analyst. From the initiation till the completion of a project, there are several risks that may arise which can have a negative impact on the business as a whole. For example, the release of a new product can be severely affected if someone from the development team is leaving. Thus, at every stage, a business analyst is required to be vigilant of what’s going on.
 User Testing
 Identifying project requirements and risks are not the only responsibilities of a BA. Instead, their main role begins when a project is underway. They have to ensure that the final product delivered to the client meets their expectations. For this, it is their responsibility to pass it through various testing scenarios. The aim of doing this is to ensure the implementation surpasses the project’s intended benefits.
 Documentation
 A business analyst spends a fair share of his time documenting his findings. Based on what they decipher, they are required to document the information into a presentation. They can do this in text or visual form including illustrations, charts and graphs.
 On an everyday basis, a business analyst is required to wear many hats. From having organisation skills to strong communication skills, there are various situations and departments in which an analyst has to coordinate. Besides the responsibilities that are entrusted to them, they also have to review company processes periodically.

Turing defined a universal computer as a formal system which, given any effective procedure, can effectively mimic the behavior of that procedure. His notion of universality was grounded in his concept of a Turing machine - an abstract model of computation that manipulates symbols on an infinite memory tape according to a specified table of rules. prompt: What is the best way for preparing for GATE CSE?
text:
Graduate Aptitude Test in Engineering (GATE) is an all-India examination which is conducted and administered by the Indian Institute of Science and some of the top Indian Institutes of Technology once in a year. Based on your GATE score one can get premiere & prestigious institutions like IISc, IITs, IIITs, top NITs, NUS, etc and jobs in PSUs.
 Aspirants who are preparing for GATE examination should concentrate on few important points:
 Analyze GATE syllabus & Weightage of each subject:
 Analyzing syllabus will help you to understand the important subjects/ topics and pattern of GATE exam.
 Syllabus of GATE for CSE is given as follows:
 Mathematics Section:
 Discrete Mathematics: Propositional and first order logic. Sets, relations, functions, partial orders and lattices. Groups.
 Graphs: Connectivity, matching, coloring. Combinatorics: counting, recurrence relations, generating functions.
 Linear Algebra: Matrices, determinants, system of linear equations, eigenvalues and eigenvectors, LU decomposition.
 Calculus: Limits, continuity and differentiability. Maxima and minima. Mean value theorem. Integration.
 Probability: Random variables. Uniform, normal, exponential, poisson and binomial distributions. Mean, median, mode and standard deviation. Conditional probability and Bayes theorem.
 Computer Science and Information Technology Section:
 Digital Logic: Boolean algebra. Combinational and sequential circuits. Minimization. Number representations and computer arithmetic (fixed and floating point).
 Computer Organization and Architecture: Machine instructions and addressing modes. ALU, data‐path and control unit. Instruction pipelining. Memory hierarchy: cache, main memory and secondary storage; I/O interface (interrupt and DMA mode).
 Programming and Data Structures: Programming in C. Recursion. Arrays, stacks, queues, linked lists, trees, binary search trees, binary heaps, graphs.
 Algorithms: Searching, sorting, hashing. Asymptotic worst case time and space complexity. Algorithm design techniques: greedy, dynamic programming and divide‐and‐conquer. Graph search, minimum spanning trees, shortest paths.
 Theory of Computation: Regular expressions and finite automata. Context-free grammars and push-down automata. Regular and contex-free languages, pumping lemma. Turing machines and undecidability.
 Compiler Design: Lexical analysis, parsing, syntax-directed translation. Runtime environments. Intermediate code generation.
 Operating System: Processes, threads, inter‐process communication, concurrency and synchronization. Deadlock. CPU scheduling. Memory management and virtual memory. File systems.
 Databases: ER‐model. Relational model: relational algebra, tuple calculus, SQL. Integrity constraints, normal forms. File organization, indexing (e.g., B and B+ trees). Transactions and concurrency control.
 Computer Networks: Concept of layering. LAN technologies (Ethernet). Flow and error control techniques, switching. IPv4/IPv6, routers and routing algorithms (distance vector, link state). TCP/UDP and sockets, congestion control. Application layer protocols (DNS, SMTP, POP, FTP, HTTP). Basics of Wi-Fi. Network security: authentication, basics of public key and private key cryptography, digital signatures and certificates, firewalls.

 Take test series:

Writing tests and practicing quality questions before attempting actual GATE will boost your confidence and improve your problem-solving speed. Since questions are analytical as well as numerical so analyze your mistakes so that you can avoid silly mistakes in final exam.

prompt: 5 dogs eat 4 steaks. Discuss the psychology of how a pack of dogs share high value food.
text:
In a pack of dogs, the sharing of high-value food like steaks is determined by their social structure, hierarchy, and individual temperaments. The psychology behind it can be broken down into the following aspects:

1. Hierarchy and Dominance: Within a dog pack, there is a social hierarchy that dictates who gets access to resources like food, mates, and territory. This hierarchy is established and maintained through various displays of dominance and submission. The alpha dog, or the most dominant member of the pack, will have the first pick of the food, while others will wait for their turn based on their rank in the group.

2. Resource Guarding: Some dogs may display resource guarding behaviors when it comes to high-value food items. This means that they will protect the food from other dogs, sometimes aggressively. They may growl, snap, or even bite other dogs that come too close to their food. This behavior can be influenced by the dog's previous experiences, their personality, and the level of competition for food within the pack.

3. Cooperation and Communication: In some cases, dogs in a pack may cooperate and share food, especially if they have a strong bond and trust each other. They communicate with each other through body language, facial expressions, and vocalizations, signaling their intentions and emotions. This communication can help maintain harmony within the group and prevent fights over food.

4. Individual Temperament: Each dog has its unique personality and temperament, which can influence how they share food within the pack. Some dogs may be more assertive and dominant, while others may be more submissive and willing to share. In some cases, a dog may be more prone to resource guarding due to past experiences or genetic predisposition.

5. Learned Behavior: Dogs learn from their experiences, and their behavior around food can be influenced by their past. A dog that has experienced food scarcity or competition may be more likely to guard its food, while a dog that has always had plenty of food and never had to compete may be more likely to share.

Overall, the psychology behind how a pack of dogs share high-value food is complex and influenced by a variety of factors, including social hierarchy, communication, individual temperament, and learned behavior. The chaining operation takes a function that operates on the raw value, and applies it to the value inside the monad, producing a new value inside the monad.

Similarly, there are monads for handling stateful computations, like the `State` monad, and for handling asynchronous operations, like the `Future` monad.

prompt: What was Late Bronze Age collapse?
text:
The Late Bronze Age collapse was a period of major societal collapse in the Mediterranean region around 1200 BCE. Many major civilizations of the age, including the Mycenaeans in Greece, the Hittites in Anatolia, and the New Kingdom of Egypt, collapsed abruptly at this time. Several factors are believed to have contributed to this collapse, including:

1. Invasions from outside groups like the Sea Peoples, who were possibly from western Anatolia or southern Europe. They attacked Egypt, Anatolia, Cyprus and the Levant.

2. Climate change and droughts which undermined agricultural production and the economies. Pollen records show major vegetation changes at this time.

3. General systems collapse - There were increasing migrations, invasions, and revolts by external groups pressing on the major empires. This weakened the empires from within and made them vulnerable.

4. Changes in military technology like the use of iron weapons which may have given external invaders an advantage over the bronze-age civilizations. 

5. Economic and trade disruptions - There were breakdowns in long-distance trade networks which these civilizations depended on. This likely led to shortages, famines and revolts.

6. Natural disasters like earthquakes - Some evidence suggests massive earthquakes may have contributed to the collapse of cities in the Eastern Mediterranean around this time.

The result was widespread destruction of cities, loss of literacy as writing systems disappeared, and a period of societal collapse and transition in the Mediterranean region in the 12th century BCE. It took several centuries for some of these civilizations to recover.

So in summary, the Late Bronze Age collapse was a "perfect storm" where climate change, invasions, natural disasters, and internal revolts coincided to disrupt societies that were heavily dependent on long-distance trade networks and agricultural production. This led to the collapse of many major civilizations in the region for decades or even centuries.

prompt: Why the sky is blue?
text:
There are a few reasons why the sky appears blue:

1. Scattering of light by particles: As sunlight travels through the atmosphere and hits tiny particles like molecules and dust particles, most of the light becomes scattered in all directions. Blue light has a shorter wavelength and is scattered more easily by these particles in the atmosphere compared to other colors. The more scattered blue light then reaches our eyes, making the sky appear blue.

2. Refraction of light: Sunlight also undergoes refraction as it enters the Earth's atmosphere at an angle and passes through air of different densities. This refracts or bends the light slightly, with blue light being refracted more than other colors - contributing to the blue appearance of the sky. 

3. Composition of the atmosphere: The composition of the Earth's atmosphere, primarily nitrogen and oxygen gases, also leads to more scattering of blue wavelengths of light compared to red or yellow wavelengths. This preferential scattering of blue light ends up making the whole sky look blue.

4. Wavelength of blue light: Blue light, with a wavelength between 400 and 490 nanometers, happens to be in the range of visibility for the human eye. Since our eyes are able to detect this wavelength of scattered light more easily, we perceive the sky as being predominantly blue.

So in short, it is a combination of factors like light scattering, refraction and the atmospheric composition that cause the preferential scattering of blue wavelengths of light - making the sky look blue to our eyes during the daytime.

Functional programming is a programming paradigm that emphasizes the use of pure functions and the avoidance of stateful objects. Here are some tips for getting started with functional programming:

1. Learn about first-class and higher-order functions: First-class functions are functions that can be passed as arguments to other functions, and higher-order functions are functions that accept functions as arguments.

2. Identify problem areas in your code: Look for places where your code is stateful, where functions rely on side effects, or where there are unnecessary computations.

3. Replace stateful code with pure functions: Replace any stateful code with pure functions that have no side effects, which can make the code easier to reason about and maintain.

4. Use recursion when necessary: Recursion is a useful technique for solving certain problems that involve depth-first search or tree traversal.

5. Avoid global state: Try to avoid using global variables that can be modified by multiple functions, as this can make the code harder to maintain and debug.

6. Use functional data structures: Functional data structures, such as lists and maps, are data structures that are designed to be pure, meaning that they don't have any side effects.

7. Practice immutability: Immutability is a core principle of functional programming, which means that functions should not modify the state of their arguments.

8. Use pure functions to build higher-order functions: By using pure functions to build higher-order functions, you can avoid side effects and make your code more modular and reusable.

9. Learn about functional programming languages: There are many functional programming languages available, such as Haskell, Lisp, Scheme, and Clojure, which can make it easier to learn and practice functional programming.

By following these tips, you can improve your functional programming skills and write more efficient, maintainable code.

prompt: Why has indexed shifting displaced traditional friction shifting on bicycles?
text:
Why has indexed shifting displaced traditional friction shifting (derailleur, shifter, bicycles)?
 I own both vintage friction shift bikes and a modern indexed shifting bikes, raced and toured during the friction shifting era and continue to put thousands of miles a year on my bikes. Based on this background I can give you two main reasons for why this happened:
When racing, a missed shift (i.e. shifting to the gap between two gears where the chain would just slide over the cogs instead of engaging in a cog) or an incorrect shift into the wrong gear could lose you the race, especially in situations like end of race sprints where split seconds counted and multiple accurate shifts were needed due to the acceleration needed at that point in the race. Index shifting (and then later shifters integrated into the brake levers) made those bad shifts a thing of the past and were a huge advantage in a sprint. Racers could not afford to stay with friction and still have a chance of winning.Many Americans who bought bikes during the ’70s to early ’80s bike boom were intimidated by the mechanical parts of bicycles, much as how many americans are intimidated by cars with manual transmissions. Especially intimidating were missed shift situations as discussed above. The loud click and tactile feedback of an indexed system was much more reassuring than the more subtle shift-then-trim-shifter-to-reduce-noise friction shifting method. This is why people flocked to Shimano’s SIS system that appeared in the early 1980s.
The very first point I made above regarding shifting to the gap between gears became a nonexistent problem after 6- and 7-speed freewheels and cassettes with shifting ramps became the norm, simply because the cogs were spaced more closely and the ramps made sure that shifts were completed.
 A significant downside to index shifting is that bikes now need “tune ups” to adjust for cable stretch that results in the index shifting not indexing properly. There’s really no need to tune up a friction shift derailleur unless you crash and bend something or change drivetrain parts.

text:
Dual numbers are a mathematical concept that extend the real numbers with an additional element called epsilon (ε), which is defined such that ε^2 = 0. Dual numbers can be written as a + bε, where a and b are real numbers.

In automatic differentiation, dual numbers are used to compute derivatives of functions. Specifically, for a function f(x), the dual number representation of x is x + ε, and the dual number representation of f(x) is f(x) + f'(x)ε, where f'(x) is the derivative of f(x) with respect to x. The key idea is that we can manipulate dual numbers like ordinary numbers, but the ε term allows us to encode the derivative information.

Example applications of dual numbers in automatic differentiation include computing derivatives of any mathematical function, including those that are difficult or impossible to differentiate analytically. For example, consider the function f(x) = sin(x^2). Using dual numbers, we can write x as x + ε, and f(x) as sin((x + ε)^2). Expanding this out and keeping only the terms with ε, we get f(x) + 2x*cos(x^2)ε, which gives us the derivative of f(x) with respect to x.

Another application of dual numbers is in optimization, where they can be used to efficiently compute gradients of objective functions. Additionally, they can be used in computer graphics to compute surface normals and curvature information for 3D models.

In summary, dual numbers are a powerful mathematical tool for automatic differentiation, allowing us to efficiently compute derivatives of functions and enabling a wide range of applications in optimization, computer graphics, and more.

from flask import Flask, render_template, request
import json

app = Flask(__name__)

    weather_data = request.args.get('weather', None)
    if weather_data is not None:
        # Parse the weather data

prompt: I have a question about programming a QScrollArea in Python 3.8 with PyQt5. I place a layout in the QScrollArea, however, the layout has extra space at the bottom beyond the size of the widgets within. How can I make layouts limit their vertical size to only the contents, to get rid of this bottom space, without making the internal widgets smaller?
text:
This extra space at the bottom of the layout is due to the QScrollArea's vertical scrollbar policy. By default, it is set to AdjustToContents, which means the scrollbar will appear only when needed.

To fix this, you have two options:

1. Set the vertical scrollbar policy to AlwaysOn. This will always show the scrollbar, and the layout will size itself to fit within the viewport of the QScrollArea:

```python
scroll_area = QScrollArea()
scroll_area.setVerticalScrollBarPolicy(Qt.ScrollBarAlwaysOn)
```

2. Set the vertical scrollbar policy to AdjustToContents (default), but call the QScrollArea's setupViewport() method after adding the layout. This will size the viewport to fit the layout contents:

```python 
scroll_area = QScrollArea()
layout = QVBoxLayout()
scroll_area.setLayout(layout)
scroll_area.setupViewport(layout)
```

So in your case, you should call setupViewport() after adding the layout to the QScrollArea:

```python
scroll_area = QScrollArea()
layout = QVBoxLayout()
# Add widgets to layout
scroll_area.setLayout(layout)
scroll_area.setupViewport(layout)
```

This will size the viewport to fit the layout contents exactly, without any extra space at the bottom.

prompt: Give an example where backpropagation is linear in the number of edges in the neural network but quadratic in the number of units in the network
text:
Backpropagation is an optimization algorithm used to train neural networks by minimizing the error between predicted and actual outputs. The algorithm computes the gradient of the loss function with respect to each weight by the chain rule, calculating the gradient one layer at a time, iterating backward from the last layer to avoid redundant calculations of intermediate terms in the chain rule.

In the case of a feedforward neural network with a single hidden layer:

1. Input layer: n units
2. Hidden layer: m units
3. Output layer: k units

The number of edges in this network can be calculated as the product of the number of units in each connecting layer plus biases:
- Edges between input and hidden layer: n * m
- Edges between hidden and output layer: m * k
- Biases for hidden layer: m
- Biases for output layer: k

Total number of edges = n * m + m * k + m + k

Now, the backpropagation algorithm computes the gradients for each of these edges, so the complexity of backpropagation is linear in the number of edges.

However, the number of units in the network is the sum of the units in each layer:
Total number of units = n + m + k

When analyzing the complexity of backpropagation concerning the number of units, we have to consider the worst-case scenario. In this case, the worst-case scenario would be when n, m, and k are of the same order, i.e., n ≈ m ≈ k ≈ N/3, where N is the total number of units in the network.

In this case, the total number of edges becomes:

Total number of edges ≈ (N/3) * (N/3) + (N/3) * (N/3) + (N/3) + (N/3) ≈ 2 * (N^2) / 9 + 2 * (N/3)

As you can see, the complexity of backpropagation concerning the number of edges is linear (O(N)). However, when considering the number of units, the complexity becomes quadratic (O(N^2)) in the worst-case scenario.

prompt: Why are scientists more concerned about the impact of CO2 in the atmosphere than water vapor?
text:
Water vapour is condensable at the temperatures found in the lower atmosphere. When its concentration exceeds about 3% of the atmosphere near the surface, it condenses and rains out of the atmosphere. As temperatures lower with altitude, it is even easier to condense the water. As a result, the water vapour percentage falls steeply above about 3 km as it condenses and is below 0.04% of the atmosphere above about 5 km. If we try to increase the water vapour concentration, it just condenses and rains out, maintaining less than 3% of the atmospheric concentration.
 Carbon dioxide, on the other hand, does not condense at temperatures and pressures found in our atmosphere. Since the atmosphere is well mixed to about 100 km, its concentration comprises about 0.04% of the atmosphere all the way from the surface to about 80 km. As we increase the amount of carbon dioxide, its concentration continues to increase since it does not condense. Since the total atmospheric concentration falls with altitude, the concentrations of water vapour and carbon dioxide fall as well. The difference is that the water vapour falls off with altitude much more rapidly. This, as explained below, makes carbon dioxide a much more potent greenhouse gas.
 Now both water vapour and carbon dioxide absorb strongly in the infrared near 15 microns. They absorb so strongly, in fact, that when they re-emit the energy it does not travel far before it is re-absorbed by another water vapour or carbon dioxide molecule. However, if that energy is re-emitted upward, it sees less water vapour and carbon dioxide (since their concentrations fall with height). Eventually the concentrations are so low that the re-absorbed energy can escape to space. However, for water vapour, the escape altitude is about 3 km, where the temperature is about -13 C, and for carbon dioxide it is about 7 km where the temperature is about -53 C.
 The Earth tries to radiate the excess energy from the Sun to space by emitting so called blackbody radiation. The wavelength at which this radiation has it strongest power is proportional to its temperature of the emitter, and the total rate at which it emits that energy is proportional to its temperature raised to the fourth power (T^4). As it turns out, the Earth is about 15 C on average, and radiates to space most strongly at about 15 microns—right where water vapour and carbon dioxide absorb. Now the water vapour re-emits that energy to space at -13 C or about 1.5 times more slowly than the Earth emits its energy. However, the CO2 re-emits that energy to space at -53 C, or about 3 times more slowly than the Earth. Thus, carbon dioxide blocks the cooling radiation to space much more effectively than water vapour. Since the rate of energy input from the Sun has to equal the rate of energy output to space to keep the temperature constant, reducing the rate energy is emitted to space in these absorption bands causes the Earth temperature to rise. It is just that carbon dioxide is better at doing this than water vapour, and because its concentration continues to increase as we add it to the atmosphere, it has a greater greenhouse effect.

prompt: Who was the first person to come up with the idea of credit score?
text:
Most laymen will tell you Bill Fair and Earl Isaac, who were the first to come up with commercially successful scores in the early 1960s. At that time, the purpose was to speed application processing, and for all intents and purposes, that has always been the case.
 SHOULD ANYBODY USE THE INFORMATION BELOW, PLEASE REFERENCE
 Anderson, Raymond [2019] Credit Intelligence and Modelling: Many Paths Through the Forest. Rayan Risk Analytics.
 The first known use of scoring was for mail order, a distance-lending enterprise lacking the luxury of personal interviews. In 1934, Spiegel implemented a ‘pointing’ system using five demographic variables—including occupation, marital status, location, and race—with points tabulated by ‘low-paid female clerks’ [Raff & Scranton 2017:276-7]. It was not for credit, but for the mailing of goods with an expectation of subsequent payment.
 At about the same time, a Phoenix bank developed a model to assess applicants with regular incomes [Dunham 1938].F†
 F†—According to Durand [1941], the published score was based on employment record (20%), income statement (25%), financial statement (10%), type of security (20%), and past payment record (25%).
 In 1935, the American Federal Housing Association issued its Underwriting Manual, which provided tables to assess the risk of prospective home loans. Besides property location and condition, the grids also assessed ‘Ability to repay’, ‘Prospects for the future’, and ‘Character’, with the latter getting the highest rating. Note, that the factors still required a subjective assessment by an individual.
 Other models were developed, with some details published. Owen L. Coon was an executive at General Finance Corporation, which specialised in automobile loans. He did an analysis of motor vehicle repossessions and developed a ‘credit quotient’ scheme for assessing loan applications, presented at a conference in 1938 [Dunham ‘38]. Joseph Greenberg was a sales finance officer (employer unknown) who published a model like the Phoenix bank's in 1940, only with more detail and greater weight on applicants’ occupation [Greenberg ‘40].
 Such practices were further adopted during World War II, as credit men were called up to serve. Before they left, they codified their rules of thumb for use by housewives employed in their stead for the war’s duration.
 Credit for the first-ever empirical (statistical) model is given to David Durand [1941], a researcher at the USA’s National Bureau for Economic Research (NBER), who noted the earlier expert models mentioned above [Dunham ’38 and Greenberg ‘41] in his paper. He was tasked towards the Great Depression’s end with assessing judgmental approaches of the era (which were quite successful considering the low loss rates). He went further to see if actuarial practices could be used for credit decisions, by applying LDA to a set sampled from 7,000 car loans obtained from banks and finance houses. He was successful, but even he doubted that it would ever replace human judgment… it remained an academic curiosity. No credit history was included (major shortcoming!), only age, gender, time at residence and employer, occupation, industry, and holding of a bank account, real estate, and/or life insurance.
 David Durand’s (1913-96) greater fame came from pioneering statistics’ and samplings’ use to explain financial markets, especially why long-term bonds yield more than short-term, in an era when computers used punch cards and sampling was a necessity. He had a BA from Cornell (34), and both Master’s and PhD from Columbia (‘41), after which he served as a lieutenant in Hawaii and Guam. He joined Princeton’s Institute for Advanced Studies, and then M.I.T. in ‘53 as a professor at its Sloan School of Management. Other consumer-credit research included farm mortgages.F†
 F†—MIT News, 28 February 1996; New York Times, 1 March 1996.
 Another unsuccessful early adopter was E.F. Wonderlic, who became director of personnel at Household Finance Corporation (HFC) in the mid-1940s. He used his knowledge of statistics to develop its ‘The Credit Guide Score’ in ‘46, which instructed analysts on the score calculation, but in ‘48 bemoaned its disuse despite substantial evidence that it worked. Credit analysts did not trust it, so instead made their decisions and dutifully calculated the score afterwards.
 Eldon F. Wonderlic (1909-80) was a psychologist better known for the Wonderlic Intelligence test, developed in 1936. After joining HFC, he tested model modifications on employees. The test was used by the U.S. Navy for selecting pilots during the war—and has since been used by thousands of companies internationally. Today, it is best known from the American National Football League, whose players’ scores are published.
 Thereafter, Sears used scoring in the 1950s to determine to whom it should send its catalogues. Being a mail-order house, it suffered from the same issues as Spiegel in terms of distance lending. Little is known about what was being predicted, but given the nature of their then business, it was likely to determine whether goods would be paid for or returned after delivery, and not as a credit score per se.
 The 1950s also saw developments in the field of operations research. Problems with logistics and resource allocation led to the development of several different methodologies, one of which was linear programming (LP). George Dantzig had come up with the interior points (or ‘simplex’) method in ‘47 while working with the U.S. Air Force, but it was not able to handle the instability of wartime environments. It was, however, perfect in stable settings, and was adopted by the Rand Corporation and U.S. Bureau of Standards during the ‘50s, and American oil companies in the ‘60s. This became the ur-methodology of today’s best-known scorecard vendor, FICO.

prompt: Could Grammarly make editors obsolete?
text:
Not right now and not until they do some serious work (probably involving AI, and even then…). It’s only an algorithm. It can only spot patterns it’s programmed to spot, and what copy editors do is far more nuanced than that.
 Frankly, if you took every suggestion Grammarly Premium gave you, much of your writing would be just as bad off (if not worse) as it was to start. To properly use Premium, you have to understand (or at least be willing to look up and learn) things like when it’s OK to use a tautology, what a dangling modifier is (and when it’s OK to leave it), specific style issues you’re expected to adhere to (not all dictionaries or outlets use the same spelling of a word — e.g., anti-fungal vs. antifungal) and that it’s not always wrong to split an infinitive (among many other things). It also can’t always determine part of speech accurately, which makes a difference. Later in this very answer, I say, “Grammarly will catch words you use too frequently…” Grammarly is telling me it should read “catchwords.” And that would be true if I said, “Using these types of catch words can confuse readers.” Because in this instance, catchwords is a noun. In my sentence, “catch” is part of the verb and “words” is a noun. More, if it falsely identifies part of speech, it can also advise you to put a comma where none belongs. And it happens frequently and many are subtler than that, meaning a novice writer wouldn’t just automatically know Grammarly was wrong.
 There are many subtleties to language it’s not able to understand. I do believe it could be set up to understand any dictionary you choose or any style guide you choose. I even believe they can make it more customizable to accommodate house style. They could even expand its capabilities to have better sensitivity to parts of speech. But there’s one problem with that.
 Fixing syntax, punctuation, and spelling aren’t all copy editors do. Text that takes you 20 minutes to read could take us an hour (depending on how many problems we identify) because we also look at the following:
Logic: Is this argument logical and cogent? Are there holes in the materials or does it rely on logical fallacies like ad hominem remarks, begging the question, slippery slopes, strawmen, or hasty generalizations?Facts: Is the text factual? Is it OK to wash raw chicken? Did the study really conclude that? Is that really how the Red Flags Rule works? Did they really say that the way you’re presenting it?Omissions: Why does this recipe say to add the green onions? There are no green onions listed in the ingredients. OK, so I should itemize my tax return if I have deductible receipts over the standard deduction amount. But what’s the standard deduction amount? How does Rachel know Taylor has the locket? She was at the doctor’s office when Ryan gave it to him and she just got back? In a mystery novel, that might be a clue. In another, it’s an omission if you don’t explain it.Overexplanation: Yes, sometimes, writers also overexplain things. Once you make your point, you have to move on. But sometimes, people do drone on and on.Inconsistencies: Earlier, you said the best rate of return you’d gotten was 5%. Now you’re saying it’s 15%? Which is it? Also, is it “internet” or “Internet”? You have to spell and style it the same way each time.Repetition: Grammarly can catch words you use too frequently in a single passage. But it can’t catch that you’ve made the same point three times unnecessarily.Organization: One of the most common problems with writing is simply organization. Things don’t flow well from point to point, there are issues with random headers that don’t have partners, the info is out of order altogether and some points would be more easily understood if you put a latter point first, etc. Grammarly’s trying to keep you from making a stupid mistake. It can’t tell you whether humans will understand your flow.Clarity: The clarity of individual sentences does not a clear point make. Clarity involves many of the other issues on this list, but essentially, when the reader is done, will they know who, what, when, where, how, and why?Word Use: Grammarly technically checks for this. But it gets a lot wrong (I’ve never once had it suggest “instead” for “rather” and had it be correct… Not. Once.). Moreover, Grammarly can’t know how certain words really work together or whether a word choice is overstated for the situation, even if it does go with that word, especially in more technical or subject matter-driven works. Just because the thesaurus tells you a word can be a synonym doesn’t mean they mean the same exact thing. I think that’s fixable, but I also think it would take a metric crapton of manpower of the professional linguist variety and many years to make it happen, and it would still be incomplete since there are subtleties and language changes so quickly and you can’t account for everything. In fact, I think that’s why they need a more robust personal dictionary/style editing system.Wordiness: Why say “in order to” when “to” works just fine? “Period of time”? Or would just “period” do? Why say, “I have an appointment with my doctor,” when you could just say, “doctor’s appointment”? If it’s “needless to say,” you don’t need to say, “needless to say” (and you might not even need to say it at all). Do you know how often I remove an irrelevant “that” from works? And those are just the common types of wordiness.Sensitivity: Grammarly can’t check your sensitivity, which can be a very important thing. It does have a tone checker, which is good for emails I guess? But sometimes, even that’s wrong. It’s just basing it on the words you use. The other day, I wrote a Quora answer about yeast and it told me I was being “forceful” the minute I started talking about how yeast dies. Good luck if you’re talking about a sensitive subject like suicide, mental health or matters of race. It can’t catch text that would be offensive when it’s subtle.Objectivity: Just because you say it well doesn’t mean it’s objective. Even if you manage to avoid logical fallacies, you can still insert bias (yes, no matter how “liberal” you think you are — no political ideology is synonymous with “objective”).Flow. Is everything presented in a logical order? Is there a variance in word usage? Do they show a mastery of the subject matter and the language? Other elements we look for cover some of this, but flow has to do with how it all works together. Grammarly can give you clues to word usage variance. But it’s often wrong. If the writer is talking about interest in terms of finance, I don’t care how many times the word is used in that passage — you still have to use it if it’s the right word, and no, interest and APR aren’t interchangeable. They aren’t the same thing. Plus, half the time, it prompts me to use something like “concern.” Moreover, repetition is also a literary device, and it’s not always wrong. And Grammarly can’t show you how it all works together.
I’m sure I’m missing something, but that at least gets the point across. I use and love Grammarly. But no, it can’t replace me right now and not for the foreseeable future.
 (As I post this, Grammarly is showing me 10 nonexistent errors (adjusted for errors it’s reading because I was using them as examples) based on the style guide I used to write it and missing a purposely introduced incorrect serial comma since the style guide I used eschews them.)

prompt: Why is it sunnier in Africa than in Europe?
text:
The difference in sunlight between Africa and Europe can be attributed to several factors:

1. Latitude: Africa is located closer to the equator than Europe, which means it receives more direct sunlight throughout the year. The equator receives sunlight at a near-vertical angle, resulting in higher solar intensity and more hours of sunlight. In contrast, Europe is situated farther north, with sunlight arriving at more oblique angles and less solar intensity.

2. Climate: Africa has a diverse range of climates, but a large part of the continent experiences tropical or arid climates, which are characterized by consistently high temperatures and abundant sunshine. Europe, on the other hand, has a more temperate climate, with a greater variation in temperature and more cloud cover, leading to less sunlight.

3. Seasonal variations: Due to the tilt of the Earth's axis, seasonal variations in sunlight are more pronounced at higher latitudes, such as in Europe. This means that during winter months, Europe experiences shorter days and less sunlight, while Africa's proximity to the equator results in minimal changes in daylight throughout the year.

4. Topography: Africa has vast open landscapes with fewer tall mountains and dense forests, allowing for more sunlight to reach the ground. Europe has more varied terrain, with mountain ranges and forests that can block or filter sunlight in certain areas.

Overall, the combination of Africa's proximity to the equator, its climate, minimal seasonal variations, and topography contribute to it being sunnier than Europe.

"Веса" и "гири" - это два важных понятия в машинном обучении и обработке естественного языка.

Каждый слой может иметь свой набор весов, который определяет, как данные снизу строятся на данные выше. Это позволяет модели лучше理解 структуру данных и делать более точные прогнозы.

В итоге, "веса" и "гири" - это два важных понятия в машинном обучении и обработке естественного языка, которые используются для определения влияния каждого элемента данных на последующий слой модели и организации слоев в модели для лучшей обработки данных.

prompt: Why aren't bullets sharp?
text:
Beyond the ball that was ramrodded into muzzleloaders, bullets took every shape and size. Single-shot rifles, even some time ago, were more accurate at longer ranges when firing a pointed bullet (bullet length, mass, and rifling is more influential to long range ballistics anyhow). But when the first repeaters were made, bullets were loaded end to end in a tube magazine. Think of a lever action 30–30. Because the bullets are end to end, you are restricted to round nose or flat nose bullets to avoid a sharp end igniting the primer in the next bullet. Additionally, having shorter rounds allowed you to load more rounds in the tube at one time (which meant stubby bullets and shorter cartridges for powder). These rifles typically only had iron sights anyway, so long range accuracy wasn’t much of a concern. Fast forward to vertical internal box magazines in bolt action rifles. You can chamber a round while lying in the prone position, the vertical magazine allows for long, pointed rounds (albeit only 3–4), and you throw a scope on top and viola, you have an accurate long range rifle.
 As far as a bullet actually being sharp, you have to understand what a bullet’s purpose is. It is not to pierce a hole in a target, it is to wreck a hole in a target, which means deforming within inches of impact. Part of that involves not being so sharp. The bullet material determines this as well, whether you have a lead bullet, partial or full copper jacket, or pure copper (there are many more bullet materials, but these are the most common). But to the point of the question, having a very sharp tip does not serve the purpose that most ammunition is made for. In fact, soldiers have been known to scrape down the tips of their bullets in order to expose and flatten the lead to make them more deadly against unarmored enemy combatants.
 Now the other bullet type we haven’t covered, handguns. Shorter barrels and iron sights limits range and velocity, especially for heavy bullets. The objective of a handgun round is not to hit a dime at 100 yards, and it is not to rip a hole through steel plate. It is to travel a very short distance, and upon impact with human flesh, flatten and deform as greatly and uniformly as possible, damaging as much tissue on its short path through the body. Round/flat/hollow bullets in handguns has nothing to do with the mechanics of loading/firing or trajectories like rifles, but has everything to do with its affect on a human target at close range.
