These cults all centred on the figure of the dying-and-resurrected god, of whom Jesus is himself an example, and often had major goddess-figures, as Mary and Sophia were for Christianity. These included the worship of Osiris & Isis, of Attis & Cybele, and the Parthian Mithras. And apart from Mithras - who was, unlike the others, a soldier’s god from the first, taken from the only enemy Rome felt her equal - these gods all had a dubious masculinity.
 Osiris is dismembered, then his parts gathered together and resurrected by his sister/wife Isis - except for his penis, which is replaced with a wooden replica to sire Horus. More than that, Osiris is a defeated god, a ‘loser’ - as in the Christianate [LINKED_TEXT: Kosovo Myth] [URL: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kosovo_Myth], a king gives up his earthly kingdom to win the kingdom everlasting. Osiris is Lord of Eternity, but became so by a passive act, an out and out defeat.
 Attis was explicitly a eunuch. His origins are even more effeminate: the hermaphroditic demon Agdistis, a primordial male-and-female entity, was feared by the gods: so they sheared off his male genitals, turning him into the goddess Cybele, the Magna Mater (Great Mother) of the Phrygians. These genitals are then incubated by a mortal woman, who gives birth to Attis, a beautiful man whom Cybele falls in love with. On seeing Cybele, Attis is overcome by the divine glory and castrates himself - after dying, he is reborn as her divine consort. All Cybele’s priests were castrated on his account (a custom banned by the Romans, who viewed effeminacy as degenerate).

Among shamanic peoples, the practice is closely associated with crossing gender boundaries - the (male) shaman acting as a woman, or simply transvestite. The custom has passed down to the hijri (man-woman, ‘transgender’) of India, closely associated with the Sufi orders carrying the traditions of old Turkic shamanism.
 To go to the early roots of Greek paganism, we find this tradition embodied in Tiresias, the blind prophet of Apollo who one might say represents the memory of this practice in Greek religion. By separating two mating serpents with his walking-stick, Tiresias is turned into a woman - and spends seven years bearing children and working as a famous prostitute. On meeting the two serpents again, he does not interfere - and becomes a man again. Later on, he is asked to resolve a dispute between Zeus and Hera on which gender enjoys sex more (both gods wanting him to say their respective gender enjoys it less) - on replying that “of the ten parts of sexual pleasure, men have only one” he is struck blind by Hera, and given the “second sight” (prophecy) by Zeus.
I don’t think I need to elaborate on this: effeminacy, & surrender of this world for the other. Another example of this figure was Odin - who sacrificed “himself to himself” on the world tree, and gave up one eye, for the secrets of the runes and prophecy. And he, too, was regarded as bridging gender boundaries - the seiðr or sorcery he brought humanity was regarded as a woman’s art.
The songs I know/ that kings' wives know not/ Nor men that are sons of men. (Hávamál)

The reason the Christians were persecuted was because they refused to sacrifice to the deified Emperor, but it was not their idea; the Hebrews had been doing the same for centuries, and the first Jew to sacrifice to the Roman gods was, tellingly, killed for it. The Romans more or less wiped out the Jews from the Holy Land (and Justinian the Samaritans, centuries later).
 Dominating psychic archetypes contain their own opposites; Jesus (and I repeat, this is the mythic Jesus we’re talking about) represented a deconstruction of the old ways, an inverted Messiah. Consider the Gospel of Matthew - by an author who saw himself as a pious, orthodox Jew - which most firmly indicts Israel for his murder.

Quoth Nietzsche, or Zarathustra - “God is dead… we have killed him. What festivals of atonement, what sacred games shall we have to invent?… There has never been a greater deed; and whoever is born after us---for the sake of this deed he will belong to a higher history than all history hitherto.”

Matthew is saying, “forget the Romans, the external enemy - forget the kingship of David. Look within yourselves, for you have blood on your hands.” I’ll get to this feeling of guilt, but this idea allowed the Christian sect to become universal and cosmopolitan, despite growing out of the most insular of tribes.
Guilt, effeminacy, and defeat - the surrender of this earthly kingdom - were the wings on which Christianity rose. Nietzsche and other “new Europe” thinkers hated it for that, as did the official Roman ideology. But this guilt was very important, because it opened a new - sufficiently new, at least - avenue to “the race of men” (as the ancient Greeks used to distinguish us from “the race of women”). There are many things wrong with any society, and especially many situations in which ancient society pushed men specifically into psychological dead ends. The pagan nobility - and the nobility were generally the most strongly attached to pagan heritage - were warriors par excellence. Many people, especially the poor, had nothing to gain from a society of wolves.
 Christianity sanctioned criticism of the clan, or the empire, or the Emperor; it allowed people to see the blood on their hands, to openly say that “something is rotten in the state of Denmark.” Most importantly, it let any man psychologically transpose himself onto Jesus, a feminine figure, and act in ways repugnant and dishonourable to the old ways. Martyrdom (i.e. meekly submitting to execution) and self-surrender were the most visible manifestations of an opening of the civilized Roman man to a new way of interacting with the world.
 The transvestite shaman breaks social and spiritual boundaries, acting as a medium between society and the spirit world. The universal sacrifice, the god who dies and is resurrected, acted as the medium to allow men the greatest collective shamanic act.
[At the time of the Crucifixion] Two other men, both criminals, were also led out with him to be executed. When they came to the place called the Skull (Golgotha), they crucified him there, along with the criminals—one on his right, the other on his left.
 One of the criminals who hung there hurled insults at him: “Aren’t you the Messiah? Save yourself and us!”
 But the other criminal rebuked him. “Don’t you fear God,” he said, “since you are under the same sentence? We are punished justly, for we are getting what our deeds deserve. But this man has done nothing wrong.”
 Then he said, “Jesus, remember me when you come into your kingdom.”

This may happen several times a day. We usually don’t need to create more than one at a time, since the new neuron integrates with our previous learnings to build on them, since we can only learn things we have some connection with. This new neuron may eventually be the basis for some future learning.

Generally speaking, hot water baseboard heating systems are more expensive to run than forced air systems, for a few reasons:

1. Energy efficiency - Hot water baseboard systems typically lose more heat to the surroundings compared to forced air systems. 3. System costs - Hot water baseboard systems generally have higher installation and equipment costs compared to forced air systems. The piping, radiators, and boilers tend to cost more.

4. Maintenance costs - Hot water systems typically have higher annual maintenance costs due to the need to service the boiler and water treatment systems. Forced air systems have lower maintenance costs.

So overall, while hot water baseboard heat can be very comfortable and long-lasting, forced air systems are generally more efficient and cost effective to operate. The higher efficiency of forced air, especially with modern heat pumps, means lower energy bills and environmental impact. But hot water heat may still make sense in some situations, like for larger homes or in very cold climates. In the end, the best system for you depends on your specific needs and priorities.

prompt: What is a covenant in terms of Australian property law?
text:
In Australian property law, a covenant is a legally binding agreement between two parties, which is usually enforceable as a contract. It is a promise or set of promises made by one party to another, which affects the use or enjoyment of land or a building.

Common examples of covenants in Australian property law include restrictions on the use of the property, such as a requirement to maintain the property in a certain condition, or to obtain the other party's consent before making certain changes to the property.

Covenants are often created when a developer or builder sells land or a building to a buyer. The developer or builder may agree to certain restrictions or obligations, such as maintaining the landscaping or common areas of the development, or providing certain services or facilities to the buyer.

Covenants can also be created by the owner of a property, which can run with the land and be binding on future owners of the property. This means that even if the original party to the covenant no longer owns the property, the covenant remains in place and is enforceable against subsequent owners.

Covenants can be beneficial to both parties, as they provide certainty and protection. For example, a developer may agree to certain restrictions on the use of the property in exchange for the buyer agreeing to certain obligations, such as maintaining the property in a certain condition.

However, covenants can also be a source of disputes between parties. If a party fails to comply with their obligations under the covenant, the other party may take legal action to enforce the agreement. It is important for both parties to carefully consider the terms of any covenant before entering into it, and to seek legal advice if necessary.

prompt: What do top-p, top-k and temperature parameters do for large language models. Give examples of what sort of values I might want to use for different applications.
text:
The `top-k` and `top-p` parameters in language models (LMs) refer to a specific way of ranking words. These parameters are used to generate a ranking of the words in the vocabulary based on their relevance to a given query. In the context of LM, `top-k` is used to generate a ranked list of words based on their relevance to a given query, and `top-p` is used to generate a top-p list of words that have the highest relevance score.
Here is an example of how these parameters might be used in generating a response to a query:
```python
import torch
from transformers import AutoModel, AutoTokenizer, AutoModelForLMHead
# Define the input prompt
prompt = input("What would you like to ask? ")
# Define the LM parameters
model = AutoModelForLMHead.from_pretrained("bert-base-uncased")
# Define the input prompt
prompt = torch.tensor(prompt)
# Tokenize the input prompt
input_ids = torch.tensor([tokenizer.encode(prompt, add_special_tokens=True)]).unsqueeze(0)
# Generate the response
output = model(input_ids)
# Get the top-k and top-p words
top_k_words = F.top_k(output, k=10, dim=1, descending=True)
top_p_words = F.top_p(output, p=0.5, dim=1)
# Print the top-k and top-p words
print(top_k_words.numpy())
print(top_p_words.numpy())
```
In this example, we defined the input prompt as "What would you like to ask?", which is a simple question that can be answered concisely. We then used the `AutoTokenizer` to tokenize the prompt and generated the output, which is a list of 10 top-k and top-p words that have the highest relevance score. In this case, we used `k=10` and `p=0.5`, but you can adjust these values based on the specific application.

prompt: What is the weirdest object you've ever found?
text:
Back in 2013 I was wondering through a remote prairie in Central Florida. In any given direction was probably five to ten miles of primarily open fields with the occasional patch of well-established hardwood tree growth. Each one an island in an ocean of golden, head-high grasses influenced by a particularly anxious May day’s winds.
 As I picked early-ripened wild raspberries into an upcycled butter bowl I happened into a particularly jurassic looking grove of old oaks, cypress and cabbage palms. On the damp forest floor were numerous hefty logs convinced to collapse many years ago by a hurricane, windstorm or perhaps just a failing root system. It was then that I spied a glistening shine coming a few inches to the right of a reluctantly rotting, black, branchless eighty foot tall-but-fallen oak trunk.
 The top quarter section of a Coca-Cola bottle protruded from the soil in a nearly horizontal fashion. The inside housed rich black dirt—the remaining exterior buried beyond sight. Immediately I considered how ridiculous that I would find garbage way out here. After a quick check of my disdain I began digging the broken glass bottle from the ground. Only, it wasn’t broken. Not even a crack. It was completely intact. A beautiful greenish crystal color. Heavy and solid. At least I wouldn’t have to be concerned about gashing open my hand or ruining a jacket pocket by transporting this refuge to a proper receptacle.
 Later, once back at the house I took my time dissolving the loam contained within the container as-well-as carefully cleaning the exterior. Grime was thoroughly caked and a superglue-like mold corroded on this thing. It had probably been out there since the 80s, I thought. At the latest the 90s. But, I was wrong. It soon became apparent that the bottle bore an embossment claiming a manufacturing date of November 16, 1915. After thorough research it was confirmed that this model of bottle only held patent from 1915 through 1922. In 1923 Coca-Cola changed the design ever-so-slightly resulting in an updated date embossment.
 That meant this soda container had been tossed away in the middle of nowhere almost one hundred years ago. At that time, the now most widely known brand around the world was twenty-four years young and the typical serving size was but six fluid ounces.
 For those of us that view liter as a scourge and disservice to the planet this story offers a glimmer of optimism. While most examples of irresponsibly discarding junk are only that, it’s nice to experience examples where a negative action can result in a glowing moment of joy.
 (Supplementum: I noticed later that new glass Coca-Cola bottles are almost exactly the same exterior size as the antique I uncovered. However, the contemporary container holds an additional two fluid ounces. The difference lies within the bottle’s wall. The 1915 specimen is much thicker. The bottom, for instance, is between 2/3rds and 8/10ths of an inch thick. That’s around three or four American quarters.)

So in summary, mild to moderate biases—especially those based on reasonable experiences and values—can provide some benefits in the right contexts and situations.  You learn to nail that F chord, and you've actually learned one way to play ANY of the 12 “major” chords on all six strings. Just slide that F up to fret 3 and you have a G major. Go up to fret 5 and you have an A major chord.

 So yeah, definitely learn this. I spent many hours just strumming F,G,F,G,F,C,F,C, etc… over and over again. Like seriously I probably played 100 hours of FGFC.

 I know bar chords are hard, but that's why they are so useful too. You will never be a decent player without learning this and it's so fundamental that you should learn it early. After a while, you'll be my age and you'll wonder why you ever thought it was even hard at all.

prompt: write the steps needed to develop a large language model
text:
1. Define the objective: Clearly outline the goals and requirements of the large language model, such as the tasks it should perform, the level of context understanding, and the desired output format.

2. Assemble a diverse dataset: Gather a vast and diverse dataset containing text from various sources, such as books, articles, websites, forums, and social media. Ensure that the dataset includes a wide range of topics and genres to train the model on different language styles and structures.

3. Preprocess the data: Clean and preprocess the dataset by removing irrelevant information, converting text to lowercase, tokenizing the text, and removing stop words and special characters. It's also essential to handle any spelling or grammatical errors present in the dataset.

4. Split the dataset: Divide the dataset into training, validation, and testing sets. The training set will be used to train the model, while the validation set will be used to fine-tune the model's parameters. The test set will be used to evaluate the model's performance.

5. Choose a model architecture: Select a suitable model architecture that can handle large-scale language understanding, such as the Transformer-based models like GPT-3, BERT, or T5.

6. Train the model: Train the chosen model on the preprocessed dataset using an appropriate loss function and optimization algorithm. Monitor the model's performance on the validation set throughout the training process to avoid overfitting.

7. Fine-tune the model: Adjust the model's hyperparameters, such as learning rate, batch size, and the number of layers, to improve its performance on the validation set.

8. Regularization and model pruning: To prevent overfitting, apply regularization techniques such as dropout, weight decay, or early stopping. Model pruning can also be applied to reduce the model's size and computational requirements, while maintaining its performance.

9. Evaluate the model: Once the model is trained and fine-tuned, test its performance on the test dataset. Use appropriate evaluation metrics, such as perplexity, BLEU score, or F1 score, depending on the specific language tasks the model is designed for.

10. Address bias and ethical concerns: Analyze the model's output for any potential biases or ethical concerns. If needed, retrain the model with a more diverse dataset or use techniques like adversarial training to mitigate these issues.

11. Optimize for deployment: Compress the model using methods like quantization or knowledge distillation to reduce its size and computational requirements, making it suitable for deployment in various environments.

12. Deploy the model: Integrate the large language model into applications, APIs, or platforms for users to access and utilize its capabilities.

13. Monitor and update: Continuously monitor the model's performance in real-world scenarios and gather user feedback. Update the model as needed to improve its performance or to address any emerging issues.

14. Iterate and improve: Continuously iterate on the model by incorporating new data, refining the architecture, and fine-tuning its parameters to enhance its capabilities and performance over time.

prompt: Are Dravidians Australoids?
text:
The simplistic racial classification of humankind based on a couple of phenotypic differences that cluster more in one region than in other (e.g. Negroid, Australoid, Caucasoid, Mongoloid etc.) is unable to account for peoples like the Dravidians (and many others) accurately. Dravidians, like others, are a highly mixed population that, genetically, represents a transition zone right at the boundary between West Eurasia and East Eurasia.
 Thus, they have a lot of ancestry and, therefore, phenotypic influence from broadly Caucasoid-looking (originally from West Asia and South-Central Asia) and broadly Australoid-looking populations (from South Asia itself, probably once extending as far as parts of Southeast Asia, too).
 They themselves show very variable relative proportions of each of them, irrespective of skin color. Some Dravidian-speaking groups, like the Iyers, are very much shifted toward the usually Caucasoid-looking West Eurasians, while others, like the tribal adivasi Pulliyar and Paniya peoples, are very much shifted toward the generically Australoid-like indigenous South Asian cluster. That means that some Dravidian speakers are probably a bit closer to a Persian-speaking Iranian or a Pashto-speaking Pashto than to a fellow Dravidian speaker from an adivasi Scheduled Tribe.
 This diversity of genetic makeup, but usually within the same pattern of some degree of mixing between West Eurasians and autochthonous South/Southeast Asians (who were originally broadly Australoid peoples in terms of phenotype), extends to the varied looks of Dravidian peoples.
ABOVE: PCA chart plotting some South Asian, West Eurasian and Southeast Asian average population samples from the HarappaWorld database. The distances between populations show their relative degree of genetic similarity.
 The Dravidians are thus unfit for all those wide-ranging and, consequently, necessarily unspecific categories that represent the extremes of each category better than those at their margins. Said categories are actually about physical phenotypes, not races in a precisely biological sense, and only indirectly, by extension, correlates with genetic origins, which can be much more varied, mixed, intricately interwoven than physical phenotypes.
 Granted, we can all see that some kinds of looks and facial features are more common (though not universal, far less exclusive) in one region’s population than in others’, but that’s still, inevitably, a very broad generalization and arbitrary definiton based entirely on people’s perceptions (therefore, inherently involving some subjectivity) on some specific potions of the looks of others (e.g. skull type, nose width and length, mouth shape and lips, whatever, the choices of main criteria to enact the classification will always be somewhat arbitrary).

prompt: What is your review of 'Dil Bechara' (2020 movie)?
text:
The emperor of all maladies has reared its pincers again. Manny – played by Sushant Singh Rajput in what tragically turned out to be his last ever on-screen performance – is afflicted with osteosarcoma, a rare tumour of the bones that has necessitated the use of a prosthetic leg. Kizie Basu (Sanjana Sanghi), on the other hand, is battling with thyroid cancer and frequently needs to lug around an oxygen cylinder (named ‘Pushpinder’, in what is just one of the many bewildering storytelling choices in this film). Both youngsters view themselves as grenades waiting to explode, fully cognizant of the fact that it’s the others around them who will need to face the resulting shrapnel.
Dil Bechara is about the interminability of that wait. As informed by Kizie in a voiceover, this is not an “ek tha raja, ek thi rani” type story: morbidity defines this film. In adapting the bestselling 2012 novel The Fault in Our Stars [and consequently the Shailene Woodley-starrer of the same name], debutant director and casting veteran Mukesh Chhabra attempts to transliterate the pathos, the overwhelming humanity of John Green’s tale into an Indian backdrop – but this is eventually a misguided effort that never really finds its footing. Indianapolis is switched for Jamshedpur, Amsterdam is replaced by Paris, “always always always” becomes “hamesha hamesha hamesha”, and an unconvincing sideplot about a has-been author is replaced by an unconvincing sideplot about a has-been musician. Here the leads bond over a shared love for music and Rajnikanth instead of a book, and poor Sushant Singh Rajput is made to utter the word ‘seri’ a dozen times so that the authenticity of his Tamilian background is never brought into question: an ill-advised choice, as you might surmise.
 Everything is highlighted with the subtlety of a Faber-Castell marker pen. “Can you please explain the seriousness of things to her?” the mother figure played by Swastika Mukherjee vents at one point, to which an oncologist – also referred to as “doctor uncle” – replies, “Travel karna bahut risky hai. Tumhara immune system weak hai.” Saif Ali Khan plays a public service announcement. “Alcohol liver ke liye kharab hai. Nahin peeni chahiye." "Cigarette sehat ke liye hanikarak hai. Cancer ho sakta hai.” The supporting characters are completely one-note here, with the pièce de résistance being a dad who keeps tripping on National Geographic for some reason. “Beer piyoge? Beer?” He later pleads with Manny, with the earnestness of a Carlsberg salesman running short of his monthly target.
 Rajput is first-rate. Ansel Elgort made for a ridiculously charismatic Augustus Waters, and channeling that delicate balance of turmoil, poise and equanimity was always going to be a difficult ask, but the late actor manages to distinguish himself yet again with a performance that’s charming and poignant in equal measure. The cigarette that he mock-smokes is a metaphor for taking Death by the horns: a cruel irony that’s unlikely to be lost on any of us.
 Sanjana Sanghi, on the other hand, is a refreshing new talent – silent, stoic and resplendent – but there’s a certain rigidity that occasionally seeps into her performance. The film unfolds through Kizie’s perspective, and her overarching outlook on life is, understandably, that of a reality show contestant waiting to be eliminated. She’s good – but then again, a Shailene Woodley she ain’t (yet).
 The biggest strength of the original film lay in its silences, in how it managed to un-sentimentalize what was, at its essence, a painfully protracted (and genuinely authentic) dance with Death. Chhabra’s direction, on the other hand, feels too staged – there is no room for nuance, and it completely lacks the verisimilitude of its predecessor. Everything feels papered over, and well, Disney-fied, and the fragility of the two leads never really comes through. There’s even an annoying DDLJ spoof thrown into the mix for good measure, and bizarre, inexplicable dialogues like “serial killers aur serial kissers ka yeh favourite spot hai” and “you’ve learnt my full name so quickly – naughty girl” don’t really help in this regard.
 Which brings us to the inevitable elephant in the room. Malignancy goes beyond tumours – and libel and witch hunts aside, we will never really know the severity of the circumstances that prompted Rajput to take the extreme step that he did. It is destined to remain his Untold Story. To paraphrase the latest fad circulating around on Twitter: the joke is not on us – we are the joke ourselves. All we can do is continue strumming our guitars in unison with him. All we can do is celebrate what was – and ponder on what could have been. India didn’t lose an emperor – but it did lose a prince.

Really what makes the difference in $$$ is your other skills and experience. If you look at job posting there are lots of posting that mention AWS experience and no cert requirements, while there are no postings with cert requirements and no AWS experience.
 The Associate Architect Cert is really just intro to AWS on a technical level. It’s not really that deep or useful by itself. What it’s good for is getting a job a company that is using AWS, but you still need the sysadmin or programming experience for these jobs. It’s sounds nice, but people in the business know what it means.
 The Professional Architect Cert is intended for people with experience in designing cloud infrastructure and apps. Studying for the cert and passing the test means you have a pretty good theoretical understand of designing AWS infrastructure and apps, but no one wants to hire an AWS Architect with zero experience. You really need additional skill sets and years of experience AWS to get a job as AWS Architect.
 The Security Cert is another good cert for $$$ (as is true for any sort of Security Cert). That said again everyone wants experience as no one wants to hire a security guy with no experience.
 The most lucrative set is going to be Associate Architect -> Professional Architect -> Advanced Security, but it’s not going to do you much good if you don’t have years of IT Security experience in the enterprise. Likewise Associate Architect -> Professional Architect -> Advanced Networking is lucrative if you have a lot IT experience in the enterprise or building large scale apps. (A starting or mid leevel IT guy with the same set of certs is not going to bring in the same pay, but it’s still a move for your career and pay.) If you are a QA guy or a Programer going the Sysops/Developer->Devops->Networking is going to bring you more $$$ and jobs than the Architect as some employer are going to pass you up as only stay long enough to get the experince to land an Architect role.
```python
import os 
from PIL import Image

# Specify the folder path containing the images
folder_path = "/path/to/image/folder"

# Get all image file names
images = os.listdir(folder_path)

# Loop through each image file 
for image in images:
    
    # Parse the image file name and extension 
    image_type = image.split('.')[-1]
    file_name = image.split('.')[0]
    
    # Open the image
    im = Image.open(os.path.join(folder_path, image))
    
    # Resize the image to half size
    half_size = im.resize((int(im.size[0] * 0.5), int(im.size[1] * 0.5)))
    
    # Save the resized image 
    half_size.save(os.path.join(folder_path, file_name + "_half." + image_type))
```

prompt: As a immigrant, how can I build my network with locals without study environment and job environment?
text:
Thanks for the A2A, [LINKED_TEXT: Rony Musabbir] [URL: https://www.quora.com/profile/Rony-Musabbir]!
 I am originally from India and I now call Australia home. When I arrived in Perth in 2015, I knew no one here. For the first 6 months, my life revolved solely around my work place and home and some trips to local places of interest – alone.
 Having lived a very social and outgoing life in India, I found it difficult at first to adjust to my new life in Perth. After spending a few weeks in a new country, one does feel overwhelmed at the shocking drop in social interaction. It’s in times like these that you need to figure out how to build a network in your new hometown. Here are a few tips from my own experiences in Australia:
 1. Your neighbors: Start with your neighbors. When you see them out and about, simply stop by to say hi and introduce yourself. You might be surprised by the response that you receive! If you are too shy for this, you may drop hand-written notes in your neighbors’ letter boxes, so when they see you next time, at least they know your name – it’s an easy way to initiate a conversation!
 2. Your local library: Visit your local library and register yourself. Look for opportunities to volunteer. Sessions like CoderDojo forums for teenagers, or basic computer classes for senior citizens are very popular at local libraries. Volunteer for such sessions.
 3. Toastmasters: Look for a Toastmasters club in your area. Your local library could have information about this. Toastmasters is a great way to improve your communications skills in a safe environment, is often open for individuals of all skill levels and is a great way to meet new people and make friends.
 4. Learn a new art/ skill: You will often find free art and craft classes advertised at your local library. Similarly your local Bunnings store will often conduct workshops for different trades. So if something like glass painting or woodwork or carpentry interests you, go ahead and make the most of such opportunities.
 5. Local neighborhood events: Visit local events in your neighborhood. These are a great way to understand which family businesses operate in your locality and give you the chance to listen to/ watch some local artists while they perform. You might also consider volunteering for such events - managing traffic on local streets or directing vehicles towards car parks etc.
 6. Sign up for a flyer distribution service: This serves multiple purposes. Firstly, if you are new to a place and are looking to make some money, this lets you do that. Secondly, you get to explore nearby localities entirely - down to every nook and corner of every street. And thirdly, while distributing flyers, you come across people mowing their lawns or walking their dogs. Chatting with people gives you the opportunity to hone your “small talk” skills and potentially lets you widen your network. Just a word of caution – it’s small talk, avoid getting too overbearing! :)
 7. Your local pub: Visit your local pub over the weekend and try to mingle with the local. More than going with an agenda of “expanding your network” you may treat this as an opportunity to learn the local culture, the lingo, the humor (I found Aussie humor pretty difficult to understand at first), the sports that the locals follow, and social etiquette in general.
 8. Meetup: The [LINKED_TEXT: Meetup] [URL: https://www.meetup.com/en-AU/] app is by far your best friend for finding people with similar interests in your vicinity. You will be surprised to see how many Meetup groups operate in your city, both - for professional as well as social purposes. Meetup groups are often the best source for meeting new people and expanding your network.
 Most importantly, understand that you are in a new place and that it will take a while for you to develop meaningful associations with people around you. In the meanwhile, be outgoing, be courteous, be respectful and most importantly, be friendly!

prompt: Tell me a story about socrates
text:
Once upon a time in ancient Athens, there lived a wise philosopher named Socrates. He spent his days roaming the bustling streets, engaging in discussions with fellow citizens about life, justice, and the nature of human existence.

One sunny day, Socrates was approached by a young man named Euthyphro, who was seeking guidance on a difficult decision he had to make. Euthyphro's father had accidentally caused the death of a worker, and Euthyphro was torn between loyalty to his father and the pursuit of justice.

Socrates, always eager to engage in philosophical discourse, decided to use this opportunity to explore the concept of piety with Euthyphro. "Tell me, Euthyphro, what is piety?" he asked.

Euthyphro, confident in his understanding of the matter, replied, "Piety is doing what the gods approve of, and impiety is doing what they disapprove."

Socrates, never one to accept an answer without probing deeper, challenged Euthyphro's definition by pointing out that the gods often disagreed among themselves on what was right and wrong. If this was the case, how could one truly know what the gods approved or disapproved of?

Euthyphro, suddenly less certain, struggled to find a satisfactory answer. Socrates continued to question him, skillfully leading Euthyphro through a series of contradictions and inconsistencies in his beliefs.

As the conversation progressed, a crowd began to gather, drawn in by the fascinating exchange between the philosopher and the young man. Socrates, always the teacher, was using his famous Socratic method – asking questions and challenging assumptions – to help Euthyphro discover the truth about piety for himself.

But as often happened with Socrates, no clear answer emerged from the dialogue. Instead, the discussion served as an opportunity for those present to examine their own beliefs and assumptions about morality and justice.

As the sun began to set, the crowd dispersed, leaving Socrates and Euthyphro deep in thought. While Euthyphro's dilemma remained unresolved, both he and the onlookers had gained something invaluable – an opportunity to reflect on their own understanding of the world and their place within it.

And so, with a nod of gratitude to Socrates, Euthyphro left to ponder his decision, while the philosopher continued his journey through the city, seeking new encounters and fresh opportunities to learn and teach through dialogue.

Throughout his life, Socrates never claimed to have all the answers, but he believed that through questioning and conversation, humans could always gain wisdom, one step at a time. And so the legacy of Socrates, the wise and humble philosopher of ancient Athens, continues to inspire and shape the pursuit of knowledge to this very day.

prompt: Why do you need to use command prompt?
text:
Command line actions are easy to automate, and make repeatable as well as scalable. Typing in commands into the command prompt might look tedious, but you can then copypaste them and/or save them into a text file (usually called a “script”), and use this text file to repeat the same set of actions again and again. You can use that text file to easily perform the same action across a thousand of servers. There are tools to automate the GUI tasks in a similar way, but they are nowhere near as reliable or easy to use.
 You can also easily reuse most of a previous command if only one thing (such as the name of the file) changed, no such option with a GUI. Imagine you need to zip some folder, move that zipped file to google drive, and then delete the source folder. If you just do it once, I bet it’s easier to use the GUI, why would anyone bother with the command line, I hear you ask. Now imagine you need to do the same thing for a different folder once every few days. With the GUI you need to do to the whole thing from scratch every time. With the command line you can reuse the previous command by copypasting it and changing just the name of the folder to apply it to, saving massive amounts of time in the long run.
 Another reason is the virtually infinite flexibility - everything that can be done with a GUI can be done from the command line, while not everything that can be done from the command line can be done from the GUI. That is because command line is closer to the messy reality of how your operating system actually works underneath, while GUI is basically a nice window dressing hiding the command line reality below.
 This leads to another important aspect - the command line is almost guaranteed to work, very important especially for rescuing computers. The GUI is basically a cherry on top of an operating system, and it requires the vast majority of the operating system to work correctly, otherwise it also fails to work. Command line, on the other hand, is one of the minimum things that an OS will have working if it manages to start at all. I’ve seen plenty of computers in my life in which GUI failed to start, but the command line worked just fine and could be used to rescue the computer. I have never seen a computer in which the command line failed to work but the GUI was fine and could be used for rescue purposes, I don’t think that’s even possible.
 Also, GUIs are costly in terms of CPU and RAM use. That doesn’t really matter on your personal computer, since its main purpose is for you to interact with it, so it would be crazy to make savings by reducing interactivity. But on a business server used to serve a website or process some data, the primary purpose is different and direct interaction with human users occurs only when necessary (software updates, backups, and such), for the most part they are to be left alone. For them it makes no sense to pay the cost of a GUI just to use it once in a few days or even weeks. That is why most servers do not have GUIs and command line is the only way to communicate with them.

```py
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

def plot_confusion_matrix(y_true, y_pred):
    plt.figure(figsize=(8, 6))
    plt.imshow(y_true, cmap='binary')
    plt.axis('off')
    plt.title('True vs Predicted')
    plt.show()
```

prompt: Is picking nose bad for health?
text:
Picking your nose is generally not advisable for several reasons:

• It can damage the delicate tissues inside the nose. The nose lining contains many tiny blood vessels that can rupture easily. Frequent nose picking can lead to nosebleeds and even infections.

• It may lead to spread of germs and infections. Your fingers can transfer bacteria and viruses into the nose. This can increase the risk of infections like sinusitis, cold, and flu.

• It can lead to spread of infections to other areas. The germs under the fingernails can spread to the nose and from the nose to other parts of the body like mouth, eyes, etc. This can potentially lead to more infections.

• It may lead to permanent nose damage. Chronic nose picking over a long period of time can lead to scarring of nose tissues, nose deformities, and even perforation of the nasal septum.

• It often becomes an uncontrollable habit. Nose picking can become an obsessive compulsive habit that is hard to stop. This habit can cause significant anxiety and embarrassment in social situations.

• It looks unhygienic and unattractive. Nose picking, especially in public, is considered rude and disgusting by many people. It leaves a bad impression on others.

So in summary, while occasional nose picking may not pose a big risk, frequent and chronic nose picking can potentially lead to various health issues and problems. It is best to keep your hands away from the nose and use a tissue to gently blow the nose when needed. See a doctor if there is any injury or infection from nose picking. Breaking the habit with determination and willpower is the best approach.

Elo rating is a system for ranking players or teams in a game or activity. The creator of Elo rating, Arpad Elo, was a Hungarian-American mathematician who developed the system in the 1930s. 
In Elo rating, each player or team is given a rating based on past performance, and then these ratings are adjusted based on each subsequent game or match. The idea is that more recent games are given more weight in the rating calculation than older games, and that the ratings will become more accurate over time as more data is collected. 
Elo rating is widely used in chess, Go, and football (soccer), among other sports. It is also used in online gaming communities and in simulated games like poker and fantasy sports.

The `` min_samples `` parameter in HDBSCAN is used to specify the minimum number of samples required to form a core sample for clustering.

A core sample is a subsample of the data that is used for clustering. In HDBSCAN, the core sample is selected based on the data points that are nearest neighbors to the seed points. The `` min_samples `` parameter controls the minimum number of nearest neighbors required to form a core sample.

When the `` min_samples `` parameter is set to a high value, the core sample will be formed by a small number of data points. This will result in a larger number of clusters being formed, as there will be more core samples. However, it may also result in some core samples being formed by a very small number of data points, which could lead to noisy or unreliable clustering results.

On the other hand, if the `` min_samples `` parameter is set to a low value, the core sample will be formed by a larger number of data points, which will result in a smaller number of clusters being formed. However, it may also result in a larger number of noise points being included in the core sample, which could lead to noisy or unreliable clustering results.

In general, the choice of `` min_samples `` will depend on the specific requirements of the data and the desired clustering results. A higher value of `` min_samples `` will result in more robust clustering results, but may also result in a larger number of clusters being formed with a smaller number of data points in each cluster. text:
Here are the steps to remove mold from wallpaper:

1. Vacuum the moldy area thoroughly to remove as much mold as possible. This will help contain the spread. 

2. Mix a solution of 1 cup bleach to 1 gallon of water. Pour the bleach solution onto the moldy area and let it sit for at least 10 minutes. This will help kill the existing mold.

3. Wipe the area clean with a damp cloth. The bleach solution should remove most of the surface mold.

4. If the mold persists, mix a stronger bleach solution of 1/2 cup bleach to 1 gallon of water. Apply this solution to the area and let it sit for at least 30 minutes. 

5. Wipe the area clean again with a damp cloth.

6. As a last resort, you may need to remove the wallpaper in the moldy area. Carefully cut out just the moldy section of wallpaper. Be sure to contain the dust.

7. Apply a fresh coat of wallpaper paste and patch the hole with a new piece of wallpaper.

8. Painting over the patched and cleaned area with mold-resistant paint can help prevent future mold growth.

The key is to first contain the mold as much as possible, kill the existing mold with bleach or a commercial mold killer, and thoroughly clean the surface. In some cases, removing and replacing the affected wallpaper may be your best option. Then apply fresh wallpaper or paint to provide a mold-resistant barrier.

prompt: I have an list of numpy arrays "prediction", every list entry has a shape of "a,b,c", where b and c are always the same but a can be variable, how can i merge them so the final shape is "x,b,c" where x is the sum of all first dimensions ?
text:
You can use np.concatenate() to concatenate the arrays along the first axis, which will sum their first dimensions:

```python
import numpy as np

# List of arrays with shape a,b,c 
prediction = [
    np.random.rand(2,3,4),
    np.random.rand(5,3,4),
    np.random.rand(1,3,4)
]

# Concatenate along axis 0 (first axis)
result = np.concatenate(prediction, axis=0)

# result.shape will be (2 + 5 + 1, 3, 4) = (8, 3, 4)
print(result.shape)
# (8, 3, 4)
```

np.concatenate() will stack the arrays along the specified axis, so in this case axis 0 which is the first dimension. This sums the first dimensions of the arrays and keeps the other dimensions the same.

prompt: Hello. I have a question. How can you prove that if A is rational, and B is irrational, A + B is irrational?
text:
That's a great question! Here's a mathematical proof:
Let A be a rational number, and B be an irrational number. We know that the sum of a rational and an irrational number is always irrational. Therefore, A + B must be irrational.
To show that A + B is irrational, we can use the definition of irrationality. An irrational number cannot be expressed as a finite linear combination of integers with rational coefficients.
If we try to write A + B as a finite linear combination of integers with rational coefficients, we get:
A + B = k1A + k2B + k3(-A) + k4(-B)
where k1, k2, k3, and k4 are integers. Since A is rational, we can write A as n/m, where n and m are integers. Then, A + B becomes:
A + B = (n/m) + (k1A + k2B + k3(-A) + k4(-B))
Simplifying this expression, we get:
A + B = (n/m) + (k1A + k2B + k3(-n/m) + k4(-m))
Notice that n/m is still a rational number, but (-n/m) is irrational because n and m are relatively prime (meaning they have no common factors). Therefore, A + B must be irrational.
Therefore, we have shown that if A is rational and B is irrational, then A + B is also irrational.

prompt: Explain Photophosphorylation
text:
Photophosphorylation is the process by which light energy is converted into chemical energy in the form of ATP. It takes place in the thylakoid membranes of chloroplasts. There are two types of photophosphorylation:

1. Non-cyclic photophosphorylation: This involves both photosystem I and photosystem II. The light energy is absorbed by photosystem II, which then passes the excited electron to photosystem I. Photosystem I then uses the light energy to generate ATP. This results in the production of both ATP and NADPH.

2. Cyclic photophosphorylation: This involves only photosystem I. The excited electron from photosystem I is recycled back to photosystem I, resulting in the production of ATP but not NADPH.

The overall steps in photophosphorylation are:

1. Light energy is absorbed by photosystem II and I, exciting their electrons.

2. The excited electrons from photosystem II are passed to photosystem I through an electron transport chain. This movement of electrons powers the pumping of protons from the stroma to the thylakoid space. This generates a proton gradient.

3. The protons then flow back down their gradient through ATP synthase, which generates ATP from ADP and inorganic phosphate.

4. NADP+ also picks up the excited electron from photosystem I and gets reduced to NADPH.

5. The electrons lost from photosystem I and II are replenished by splitting water molecules. This also produces protons and oxygen gas. 

So in summary, photophosphorylation converts light energy into chemical energy in the form of ATP and NADPH, which are then used in the Calvin cycle to convert carbon dioxide into glucose.

prompt: Explica por qué no es viable realizar un ataque de "double-spending" si el atacante no dispone del 51% de la potencia de cálculo total del sistema Bitcoin
text:
Un ataque de double-spending (gastar el mismo bitcoin dos veces) no es viable si el atacante no tiene al menos el 51% de la potencia de cálculo total del sistema Bitcoin por las siguientes razones:

1. Para realizar un ataque de double-spending, el atacante debe poder revertir una transacción ya confirmada en la blockchain de Bitcoin. Para ello, necesita generar una cadena alternativa más larga que la cadena original.

2. La longitud de la cadena blockchain se determina por la potencia de cálculo total de la red. Cuanto más nodos mineros haya resolviendo bloques, más rápido se genera la cadena.

3. Si el atacante no tiene al menos el 51% de la potencia de minería total, no podrá generar una cadena alternativa más rápido que el resto de la red trabajando de forma honesta. Por lo tanto, no podrá revertir transacciones ya confirmadas.

4. El requisito del 51% se conoce como "umbral de seguridad" y asegura que la cadena generada por la mayoría honesta de la red siempre será la cadena válida y prevalecerá sobre cualquier cadena alternativa.

En resumen, sin al menos el 51% de la potencia de minería total, un atacante no podría generar bloques lo suficientemente rápido como para revertir transacciones ya confirmadas y realizar un ataque de double-spending. El sistema Bitcoin está diseñado de forma que se requiere al menos el 51% del hashrate total para llevar a cabo este tipo de ataques.

prompt: In what ways was Christianity morally superior to the paganism it replaced?
text:
I struggle to find so many ways in which Christianity was morally superior to the paganism of the early Roman Empire: at best I would call it a draw. Later Christians believed all kinds of atrocities had occurred in pagan times, but there is little evidence of this:—
 Rome was a centre for gladiatorial contests and cruel blood sports, which the Greeks deplored, preferring athletics, art and theatre. The gladiatorial contests and Roman blood sports were eventually banned in the Christian empire, but Christians found new blood sports, such as bull-fighting, bear-baiting and cock-fighting.
 Unlike the Christians who came afterwards, the pagan leaders were generally religiously tolerant. There were some brief periods of official persecution of Christians, usually because the Christians appeared disloyal to the empire or brought about natural disasters by their lack of respect for the gods. In any case the extent of persecution appears to have been exaggerated by Christian tradition. Edward Gibbon says, in The Decline and Fall of the Roman Empire that the Christians of the fourth or fifth centuries created these exaggerated traditions in order to justify their own persecution of the pagans:
The ecclesiastical writers of the fourth or fifth centuries ascribed to the magistrates of Rome the same degree of implacable and unrelenting zeal which filled their own breasts against the heretics or the idolaters of their own times.
It is true that the Greeks encouraged homosexual relationships with adolescent youths, but they despised homosexual relationships among grown men. The Romans looked down on homosexuality, but did not ban it. Today, we no longer generally regard homosexual relationships as immoral, but for those who do this would be one example of Christian moral superiority.
 Christianity came out of a Jewish milieu in which polygamy was permissible, but when it spread to the Greek-speaking territories of the empire and to Rome itself, it was forced to accept the pagan view that polygamy is immoral.

prompt: What is on-page SEO?
text:
On-page SEO, also known as on-site SEO, refers to the optimization techniques and practices implemented directly on a website to improve its visibility and search engine rankings. It involves various factors and elements that can be controlled and modified within the website itself. Here are some key aspects of on-page SEO:
 Keyword Optimization:
 Conducting keyword research and strategically placing relevant keywords in page titles, headings, meta tags, URLs, and throughout the content to help search engines understand the topic and relevance of the page.
 Content Quality:
 Creating high-quality, informative, and engaging content that satisfies user intent. This includes ensuring the content is unique, well-structured, and offers value to the readers.
 Meta Tags:
 Writing compelling meta titles and meta descriptions for each page, incorporating relevant keywords, and providing concise summaries that entice users to click through to your website from search engine results pages (SERPs).
 URL Structure:
 Using clean and descriptive URLs that include relevant keywords makes it easier for search engines and users to understand the page's topic.
 Heading Tags:
 Utilizing heading tags (H1, H2, H3, etc.) to structure the content and highlight important sections, incorporating keywords where appropriate.
 Internal Linking:
 Creating internal links within your website to connect related content and help search engines crawl and understand the structure of your site. This also helps users navigate through your website easily.
 Image Optimization:
 Optimizing images by using descriptive filenames, alt tags, and compressing file sizes to improve page load speed and enhance accessibility.
 Page Load Speed:
 Ensuring that your web pages load quickly by optimizing image sizes, minifying CSS and JavaScript files, leveraging browser caching, and using content delivery networks (CDNs) if necessary.
 Mobile-Friendliness:
 Designing and optimizing your website to be mobile-friendly and responsive, as an increasing number of users access the internet through mobile devices.
 User Experience:
 Creating a positive user experience by organizing and presenting content in a user-friendly manner, with easy navigation, clear calls-to-action, and intuitive design.
 These on-page SEO techniques, when implemented effectively, can help search engines better understand your website's content and relevance, leading to improved rankings and visibility in search engine results.

prompt: Is it possible to achieve native fluency as an adult with no prior experience in a language without living in a country where it is the primary language (for any period of time)?
text:
Sure, it happens to immigrant kids somewhat commonly. The parents speak language A from the old country at home with the kid, and the kid hears language B at the new country. So now the kid becomes a native-speaking bilingual of languages A and B. No matter how uncommon language A may be in the new country, and even if the kid hadn't visited the old country.
 Granted, the kid may be a bit less functional in language A for some things since they won't be receiving their instruction in it most likely, but the kid still can function in it decently well. Take them to the old country and they won't be very lost at all in using language A even for those things for very long.
 If you don't believe me, I have a friend who exactly fits this description.
 Edit — I missed the part of being an adult. That ship sailed if you had no exposure as a kid — adult learners of a language are never native speaking by definition. Adult learners probably could try to learn without going to another country through immersion if they can meet native speakers outside where it's a primary language, but that won't be too easy to find, necessarily. And again, it only can get good fluency, not native fluency.
